findings.finding: 'This adapter around the OpenRouter Agent SDK (to be built ...). Which to build first is not yet decided' is false. The adapter exists (adapters/openrouter-acp/src/adapter.ts) and is listed first in the harness catalog (crates/roundtable-web/src/tables.rs:76-99). This also contradicts the document's own elephant.built.

'Serves the ACP agent side for any OpenRouter model id' is false. Only catalog models that list 'tools' and are served on /api/v1/responses are offered (adapters/openrouter-acp/src/models.ts:36-71). set_config_option rejects any other value (adapter.ts:245-251). session/new fails if openrouter/auto is missing from the catalog (adapter.ts:214-219).
'Routes chat completions': the SDK's callModel calls the Responses endpoint, POST /api/v1/responses (adapters/openrouter-acp/src/models.ts:19-20; adapter.ts:150-161).

'Keeps its file tools inside the session folder' holds for read_file, list_directory and write_file (tools.ts:113-125, 135-146, 411-415). It leaves out that run_command runs `/bin/sh -c` in the session folder with no path confinement and no time limit. Only OPENROUTER_API_KEY is removed from its environment, and cancelling kills the whole process group (tools.ts:248-264, 277-287, 431-453). write_file and run_command ask for permission first (tools.ts:204-229).

The ACP surface and its limits are undocumented: ACP v1 (adapter.ts:3); loadSession false; no MCP over HTTP or SSE (adapter.ts:173-183); prompts accept only text and resource_link (adapter.ts:76-90); one turn at a time per session (adapter.ts:259-261); OPENROUTER_API_KEY required (adapter.ts:127-136); additionalDirectories refused (adapter.ts:196-198); the SDK's hour-long retry is turned off (adapter.ts:229-231); a new session starts on openrouter/auto (models.ts:17).

The investigation says the adapter is 'to be built' and the route is undecided between Pi and this adapter. The elephant layer says it is built and the owner chose OpenCode. The stale investigation leaves the element's status unclear.
'Refuses tool servers' and 'Roundtable tools' are undefined; a reader can't tell what is refused, how, or what seats lose.
The owner quote uses the undefined name 'ori'. 'Rarely used' is vague: is it still selectable, by whom, and is it kept or retired?
Wants both the gateway (chat completions) and the SDK (agent loop) without saying whether OpenRouter is called directly or only through the SDK.
'agent host library' and role 'SE' are undefined.

paraphrase.egm-codebase-details: adapters/openrouter-acp is a Node ACP v1 agent. It wraps the OpenRouter Agent SDK so a Roundtable seat can run an OpenRouter model through the normal ACP session lifecycle. Each session keeps its own conversation state and a `model` select option filled from OpenRouter's catalog. The model gets four tools defined by the adapter (read_file, list_directory, write_file, run_command), with permission requests for writing files and running commands.
paraphrase.egm-comprehension: A separate ACP agent binary (adapters/openrouter-acp) that wraps the OpenRouter Agent SDK so any OpenRouter model id can join as a participant through the normal ACP lifecycle. It exists, refuses tool servers and keeps file tools inside the session folder. The owner has since routed OpenRouter models through OpenCode, so it is rarely used.

roundtable.resolution:
# Resolution of review findings — `code.adapter.agent` (OpenRouter ACP adapter)

## Method and scope

I read the description (`element.md`) and all five source files copied into
`source/adapters/openrouter-acp/src/`: `adapter.ts`, `models.ts`, `tools.ts`,
`index.ts`, `sdk-patch.ts`. Line-by-line verification of every code claim made by
the reviewers is in `ShadowMortar-evidence.md`.

The code is the ground truth for this review: the reviewers read "the description
above and the code", and the findings' central claims check out, subject to the
GF4 confinement qualification below. GF1's citation of `crates/roundtable-web/src/tables.rs:76-99` is
**not** in the provided `source` folder and cannot be verified here; it is
supplementary, not load-bearing, for that finding.

**Headline decision: all ten findings are Right.** The code is consistent and its
non-obvious behaviours are already explained in its own comments; what is wrong,
stale, or vague is the **description** (`element.md`). **Every fix is to the
description. No source-code change is required to resolve any finding** (the one
optional code considerations, GF4, are noted below). Related findings share edits;
the consolidated six-step plan below avoids applying the same correction twice.

| # | Severity | Verdict | Fix lives in |
|---|---|---|---|
| GF1 | Blocker | Right (one citation unverifiable) | `element.md` investigations |
| GF2 | Blocker | Right | `element.md` wants (client) |
| GF3 | Blocker | Right | `element.md` wants (gateway) |
| GF4 | Major | Right | `element.md` elephant.built (+ optional code) |
| GF5 | Major | Right | `element.md` new ACP-surface section |
| GF6 | Major | Right | `element.md` investigations (same edit as GF1) |
| GF7 | Major | Right | `element.md` elephant.gaps |
| GF8 | Major | Right | `element.md` elephant.gaps |
| GF9 | Nit | Right | `element.md` wants (same edit as GF3) |
| GF10 | Nit | Right | `element.md` properties |

---

## GF1 — Blocker, investigations "build or reuse" — **Right**

**Why.** `element.md:46` says the adapter is "(to be built …)" and "Which to build
first is not yet decided". That is contradicted by (a) the code itself:
`createAdapter` in `source/adapters/openrouter-acp/src/adapter.ts:118-301` is a
complete ACP implementation, with `index.ts` wiring it to stdio; and (b)
`element.md:70` (`elephant.built`) which says it *is* built. The description is
internally inconsistent about the element's current status.

Two caveats that keep this honest:
- The claim that the adapter is "listed first in the harness catalog
  (`crates/roundtable-web/src/tables.rs:76-99`)" cannot be checked from the provided
  source folder; that file is absent. The finding stands without it, because the
  source and `elephant.built` already prove the adapter exists. The editor should
  confirm that catalog line before repeating the "listed first" detail.
- `investigations` are point-in-time notes. The right resolution is to mark the
  build-vs-reuse question **resolved**, not to claim the old observation was always
  false.

**What to change.** Replace the `investigations` note (`element.md:46`) with a
resolved statement, e.g.: *"Two routes were considered: Pi + pi-acp (existing) and
this adapter around the OpenRouter Agent SDK. The adapter was built
(`adapters/openrouter-acp`, see `elephant.built`); one adapter serves every model
id that passes the catalog filter in `models.ts`. The build/reuse question is
therefore settled. Note the later owner decision recorded in `elephant.gaps`
(2026-11-06): the author's account reports that the owner preferred OpenCode for
OpenRouter models. This does not establish usage frequency or retirement."*
This single edit also resolves GF6.

---

## GF2 — Blocker, wants relied on by `code.client.agent` — **Right**

**Why.** `element.md:17` claims the adapter "Serves the ACP agent side for **any**
OpenRouter model id". The code does not:
- `fetchModelOptions` (`models.ts:43-80`, filter at `:66-68`) keeps only catalog
  models whose `supported_parameters` contains `"tools"` **and** whose `endpoints`
  contains `"/api/v1/responses"` (`models.ts:20`). There is no built-in list; the
  catalog is fetched per session (`models.ts:4-5`).
- `session/set_config_option` rejects any value not in that set
  (`adapter.ts:245-251`).
- `session/new` fails outright if `openrouter/auto` (`INITIAL_MODEL`,
  `models.ts:17`) is not in the filtered catalog (`adapter.ts:214-219`).

"Any" is an overclaim: arbitrary or filtered-out ids are refused. The filtering is
deliberate and correct (a model without tool support or without the Responses
endpoint would fail on the first prompt — `models.ts:38-41`), so the code should not
change.

**What to change.** Qualify `element.md:17` to say the adapter serves the ACP agent
side for the OpenRouter model ids it offers, i.e. those passing the catalog
filter (`tools` + `/api/v1/responses`); `session/set_config_option` rejects any
other value, and `session/new` requires `openrouter/auto` to be present. Keep the
`send_receive` intent. This is the fix; do not "fix" the code to accept all ids.

---

## GF3 — Blocker, wants `upstream.gateway.llm` "Routes chat completions" — **Right**

**Why.** The code never uses chat completions. `runTurn` calls `callModel`
(`adapter.ts:150-161`) with an `input_text` payload — the OpenRouter **Responses**
format — and `models.ts:19-20` records the endpoint as `POST /api/v1/responses`.
A grep of all five source files finds no `chat/completions`. The word "chat
completions" in the description is also a leftover from the old Python path: the
`archaeology` layer (`element.md:55`) says Python "called OpenRouter models directly
through chat completions, outside ACP". The ACP adapter replaced that with the SDK's
Responses calls, so the description mixes the retired and current call paths.

**What to change.** Rewrite the `upstream.gateway.llm` `Function` (`element.md:20`)
to reflect the Responses endpoint and the SDK, e.g. *"Routes model inference to the
selected provider model via the OpenRouter Responses endpoint
(`POST /api/v1/responses`); inference is invoked through the OpenRouter Agent SDK.
The adapter separately fetches the model catalog directly."* Also
reconcile with GF9 (below). No code change.

---

## GF4 — Major, `elephant.built` "keeps its file tools inside the session folder" — **Right**

**Why.** `element.md:70` states a containment guarantee that is only partly true and
therefore misleading. Verification:
- `read_file`, `list_directory`, `write_file` validate paths: `resolveInRoot`
  (`tools.ts:113-125`) does lexical + symlink-aware resolution (including dangling
  links, `:71-100`) and `openResolved` uses `O_NOFOLLOW` (`:135-146`); `write_file`
  re-checks after the permission round-trip (`:411-415`). These checks reject
  lexical escapes and symlink escapes on a stable filesystem. They are not a
  race-proof confinement guarantee: `O_NOFOLLOW` protects only the final path
  component, parent directories can change after validation, and listing uses
  pathname-based `fs.readdir` (`:367`).
- `run_command` is **not** covered by that statement. `runShell` (`tools.ts:254-306`)
  runs `/bin/sh -c` with `cwd` = session root but **no path confinement** (the
  command can reference any absolute path), **no time limit** (explicit at `:252`),
  withholds **only** `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` from the environment
  (`WITHHELD_ENV`, `:34`, `:257`) — so *other* environment secrets are exposed to
  model-run shell commands — and on cancel kills the whole process group with
  `SIGKILL` (`:277-287`). `write_file` and `run_command` both call
  `session/request_permission` first (`needsPermission:true` at `:396`, `:443`;
  lifecycle `:204-229`). All accurate.

**What to change — narrow the claim, do not negate it.** The reviewer's finding is
right that the statement is incomplete. The three file tools have real path
checks, but their confinement claim needs the filesystem-race qualification above;
the shell has no such checks. Writing "the adapter does not check paths" would *understate* real,
careful protections and could mislead a maintainer into "fixing" working code. Make
`elephant.built` precise instead of a blanket claim, e.g.:
*"…It rejects client-supplied MCP/tool servers. Its three file tools (read_file,
list_directory, write_file) check paths against the session folder using symlink-aware
resolution (including dangling links), with O_NOFOLLOW on read/write final components and write_file re-checking
after the permission prompt; the fourth tool, run_command, runs `/bin/sh -c` in the
session folder but is **not** path-confined, has no time limit, withholds only
OPENROUTER_API_KEY from the environment (other environment secrets remain visible
to model-run commands), and is killed as a process group on cancel; write_file and
run_command require client permission **per invocation, not per session**."*

A concrete probe discriminates the two readings (verified against the code): in a
session rooted at `/root/s`, `read_file` with `../../etc/passwd` is refused by the
lexical check in `resolveInRoot` (`tools.ts:114-117`) inside `prepare`
(`tools.ts:336`) before any permission prompt — no `tool_call` reaches
`in_progress` — whereas `run_command` with `cat /etc/passwd` **succeeds once the
client grants permission and host filesystem permissions permit the read**, because its `prepare` (`tools.ts:445-451`) does no path
resolution. (Precision: a `tool_call` "pending" notification is emitted at
`tools.ts:194-197` before `prepare` in both cases; only the `in_progress` update at
`:231` is never reached for the refused read.) The security-relevant fact to record
is that this adapter's shell gate is a selected `allow` permission response on each
call. The ACP client supplies that response; the source does not establish that a
human must click. Host OS permissions and any external sandbox still apply.

**Permission granularity.** `createTools` is rebuilt on every `session/prompt`
(`adapter.ts:158`, inside `runTurn`), and `lifecycle` issues
`session/request_permission` with `allow_once` / `reject_once` on **every** call
(`tools.ts:204-229`, options at `:216-219`). So the gate is per tool invocation,
not a session-wide grant; a model can prompt repeatedly. The description must say
so, or a reader will assume a stronger, cached control than exists.

**Code:** no change is required to resolve this finding — the behaviour is
intentional and documented in `tools.ts`. But the editor should be aware that if
"keeps its file tools inside the session folder" was meant as a real security
property, the code has a genuine gap (unconfined `run_command`, no timeout, one-key
env filtering, and file-path races); adding stronger isolation or a timeout would
be a *separate design/code task*. A session-wide permission grant is not a
confinement fix and would broaden authorization rather than strengthen isolation.

---

## GF5 — Major, whole document — undocumented ACP surface and limits — **Right**

**Why.** All nine items are real, externally visible behaviours of the code, none of
which appear anywhere in `element.md`:

| Limit | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Implements ACP **v1** | `adapter.ts:3` |
| `loadSession: false` | `adapter.ts:176` |
| no MCP over HTTP or SSE | `adapter.ts:178` (`mcpCapabilities:{http:false,sse:false}`) |
| prompts accept only `text` and `resource_link` | `adapter.ts:76-90` (`promptToText`, default throws) |
| one turn at a time per session | `adapter.ts:259-261` |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` required | `adapter.ts:127-136`, called `:186`,`:258` |
| `additionalDirectories` refused | `adapter.ts:196-198` |
| SDK's hour-long retry disabled | `adapter.ts:229-231` (`retryConfig:{strategy:"none"}`) |
| new session starts on `openrouter/auto` | `models.ts:17`, used `adapter.ts:224` |

A functional map "records what each part must do … and knowledge about it"
(`element.md:3`), so the advertised ACP contract (capabilities, limits, required
env, turn model) belongs here; a reader of the current description cannot know any
of it.

**What to change.** Add a concise "ACP surface / contract" section (or a new `acp`
layer) to `element.md` capturing the table above, prioritising the externally
visible contract (ACP v1, capabilities advertised in `initialize`, one-turn model,
`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, model selection/filter, default model). It should be a short
structured summary, not a paste of every implementation detail. No code change.
This edit overlaps GF2 (model filter) and GF7 (MCP/tool servers); keep them
consistent.

---

## GF6 — Major, comprehension — investigations vs elephant — **Right**

**Why.** `element.md:46` says "to be built" and the route is "not yet decided"
between Pi and this adapter; `element.md:70` says built; `element.md:73` records the
owner's 2026-11-06 decision to move OpenRouter models to OpenCode. Three layers
give three different impressions of status, leaving the element's state unclear.

**What to change.** Same single edit as GF1: resolve the investigation note, record
that the adapter was built, and cross-reference the OpenCode decision in
`elephant.gaps`. Do not leave the stale "not yet decided" text alongside it.

---

## GF7 — Major, comprehension — `elephant.gaps` undefined terms — **Right**

**Why.** `element.md:72` says seats "get no Roundtable tools, because it refuses
tool servers". Neither term is defined, and a reader cannot tell what is refused or
what is lost. The code is concrete: `session/new` rejects any non-empty `mcpServers`
(`adapter.ts:190-194`, "this adapter does not connect to client-supplied MCP
servers") and `initialize` advertises `mcpCapabilities:{http:false,sse:false}`
(`adapter.ts:178`). The only tools a seat gets are the four built-ins in
`tools.ts:455` (`read_file`, `list_directory`, `write_file`, `run_command`).

**What to change.** Define the terms in `elephant.gaps`: "tool servers" = client-
supplied MCP servers, which `session/new` rejects (`adapter.ts:190-194`) and which
the adapter does not advertise (`adapter.ts:178`); "Roundtable tools" = the
harness-provided tools delivered over MCP, which these seats therefore cannot use;
they get only the adapter's four built-in tools when created with `mcpServers: []`.
If the client instead supplies servers, session creation fails rather than silently
creating a seat without those tools. When stating that `run_command` is
permission-gated, add **per invocation, not per session** (see GF4) — `createTools`
is rebuilt each prompt (`adapter.ts:158`) and `allow_once` is requested each call
(`tools.ts:216-219`), so there is no cached session grant. No code change.

---

## GF8 — Major, comprehension — `elephant.gaps` quote and status — **Right**

**Why.** `element.md:73` uses the undefined name "ori" and the vague "rarely used",
without saying whether the adapter is still selectable, by whom, or whether it is
kept or retired. The description gives no way to answer those questions.

**What to change.** Remove the informal quote; the supplied materials do not define
"ori", so do not invent an expansion. Attribute the OpenCode preference to the
author's account. Replace "rarely used" with a sourced concrete status
statement (still selectable / kept as a fallback / retired, and who can choose it).
Note: whether it remains in the harness catalog is the `tables.rs` claim from GF1,
which cannot be verified from the provided source — the editor should check that
file before asserting selectability. Until verified, say: "The adapter implementation
remains present; current selectability, usage frequency, and retention or retirement
policy are not established by this snapshot." No code change.

---

## GF9 — Nit, comprehension — wants gateway + SDK — **Right**

**Why.** `element.md:19-21` lists two wants: `upstream.gateway.llm` ("Routes chat
completions", `send_receive`) and `upstream.sdk.agent` ("agent loop, tool execution
and conversational state", `receive`), without saying whether OpenRouter is called
directly or only through the SDK. The code resolves the ambiguity: the adapter
constructs `OpenRouter` from `@openrouter/agent` with a custom `HTTPClient`
(`adapter.ts:226-232`) and calls `callModel` (`adapter.ts:150`) for inference.
However, `fetchModelOptions` directly calls `fetchImpl` for the OpenRouter catalog
(`models.ts:49-53`), including pagination. Inference goes through the SDK on the
Responses endpoint; catalog retrieval goes directly through the supplied fetch.

**What to change.** With GF3, collapse the ambiguity: state that this element reaches
OpenRouter inference via `@openrouter/agent`'s `callModel` (Responses endpoint),
with a separate direct catalog GET;
describe the gateway want as the OpenRouter inference service and the SDK want as
the agent loop/tools/state, and drop "chat completions". Keep both wants if the map
needs them, but make the direct-vs-SDK relationship explicit. No code change.

---

## GF10 — Nit, comprehension — properties undefined — **Right**

**Why.** `element.md:8` `"package": "agent host library: separate ACP agent binary
(reusable)"` and `:11` `"role": "SE"` are undefined labels; the document never
explains "agent host library" or what "SE" denotes. They are accurate only to
someone who already knows the project's vocabulary.

**What to change.** Define packaging as a separately launched ACP stdio agent
process with a reusable TypeScript `createAdapter` factory. Expand `SE` using the
map's authoritative role legend, link that definition, or remove the code if optional.
Calling `SE` a "role code" alone does not explain its meaning; the supplied files
do not establish its expansion. No code
change.

---

## Consolidated edit plan for `element.md`

1. **Investigations** (`element.md:46`) — resolve build/reuse; adapter built;
   cross-reference the OpenCode decision. *(GF1, GF6)*
2. **Wants** (`element.md:17,19-21`) — qualify "any model id" with the catalog
   filter; replace "chat completions" with the Responses endpoint; state that
   inference uses the SDK while catalog fetching is direct. *(GF2, GF3, GF9)*
3. **elephant.built** (`element.md:70`) — **narrow, do not negate**: describe the real
   path checks of the three file tools with their race limitation, add an explicit non-confinement sentence for
   `run_command`, and state the permission gate is per invocation, not per session.
   *(GF4)*
4. **elephant.gaps** (`element.md:72-73`) — define "tool servers"/"Roundtable
   tools"; remove unexplained "ori"; give sourced status or explicitly record it
   as unverified. *(GF7, GF8)*
5. **New ACP-surface section/layer** — ACP v1, advertised capabilities, prompt
   types, one-turn model, required key, refused params, retry policy, default
   model. *(GF5, consistent with 2 & 4)*
6. **Properties** (`element.md:8,11`) — define or drop "agent host library" and
   "SE". *(GF10)*

## On the code

**No source change is required to resolve these description findings.** The
description must accurately record the implementation's limits. GF4 identifies
possible future code work: shell isolation, timeout/environment policy, and
race-resistant file access if strict filesystem confinement is required. Existing
comments establish intended behavior; they do not prove the absence of bugs.

## Unverifiable item to confirm before publishing

GF1's "listed first in the harness catalog (`crates/roundtable-web/src/tables.rs:
76-99`)" — that file is not in the provided `source` folder. Verify it in the full
repo before repeating the claim or using it to answer GF8's "still selectable"
question. It does not affect the verdict on GF1.

CrypticComet's additional source-based corrections to the shared decisions are
documented in `CrypticComet-evidence.md`: direct catalog access, file-path race
limits, permission-response semantics, and unsupported status/terminology claims.

decisions.decision: ACP sessions keep their own conversation, so each turn prompt carries only what is new since that participant's last turn: accepted contributions with canonical ids, its own pending disposition (veto reasons, characters removed), its allowance, and the topic when it changed. The full rendered prompt of every turn is stored in the discussion record.
The turn prompt states the reply convention (contribution text, PASS, or WORK on the first line) in one short line, alongside the owner's participant prompt rather than inside it.

decisions.status: per owner statements; wording open for owner
decisions.decision: The first turn prompt asks the group to agree a strategy for the objective: how they will coordinate, whether to divide the work or each pursue it with its own strategy, and suggests they elect a head of the table who can choose for the group. Strategy contributions go through the normal loop; no extra phase or gate.

The prompts explain the two participant tools in plain words: advance (normally used by the head of the table to end the current topic, optionally naming the next) and feedback (rate another participant's behavior; ratings build accolades and identity). The tools have no role checks.

Chair guidance is delivered to every participant in its next turn prompt, marked as from the chair. It is not judged by JEV: the gate exists to protect participants' attention from each other, not to filter the person they work for.
The 'You have N Characters to Respond' line is not sent.
decisions.owner_statement: I prefer not to have the message that reads "You have 512 characters to reply.. I dont like that popping up

rules: Each discussion turn starts with the round line: 'Round N of T', then '3 Rounds Remain', '2 Rounds Remain', '1 Round Remains', 'Final Round'; 'Round N' with no limit.
Then the agent's own rejection reasons, if any, then each other agent's new accepted message as '[R1-2] Name: text'.
No characters line and no instruction to reply.
The first turn is the owner's roundtable prompt with the owner's participant prompt inside it and the first turn after 'Current delivery:'.

# Participant turn prompt — review resolutions

Decisions by SmoothShift, 2026-11-07. This resolves the findings; it does not implement the proposed source or description edits.

## Evidence and precedence

The supplied snapshot contains only `source/crates/roundtable/src/turn.rs` and `prompts.rs`. Resource templates, `engine.rs`, `rules.rs`, and the referenced engine document are absent. References below use paths relative to `source/crates/roundtable/`. Assertions about absent files are identified rather than presented as independently verified.

The owner's explicit no-characters-line decision and the active rule against a generic reply instruction take precedence over older conflicting decisions. Preserve the owner-authored templates. A historical decision must be marked superseded or unimplemented when it does not describe current behavior; merely leaving it in the decisions list perpetuates the contradiction.

## Individual findings

### GF1 — Accept the contradiction; change the description

`turn_prompt` adds no PASS/WORK instruction (`src/turn.rs:31–83`). The stronger claim about all resource text cannot be checked from this snapshot. Nevertheless, the reply-convention decision directly conflicts with the active “no instruction to reply” rule.

Mark the November 5 reply-convention decision superseded by that rule. State that the builder emits no generic contribution/PASS/WORK instruction. Do not restore one to satisfy a stale decision. Parser behavior belongs in the reply-handling description and must be verified separately; recognizing a control value does not establish that this builder must advertise it.

### GF2 — Accept the implementation gap, with a resource-evidence limit

Neither source file constructs kickoff strategy guidance or explains `advance` and `feedback`. Electing a head, as quoted by the reviewer, does not ask participants to agree how to coordinate. The absent templates prevent independently confirming the categorical claim that no prompt contains this material.

Retain the explicit kickoff and tools decisions as intended requirements, but label them unimplemented in the supplied builder. Unlike the allowance and reply-convention decisions, there is no explicit later owner prohibition of strategy or tool guidance. Close the gap by adding concise first-turn guidance in the builder's delivery, outside the verbatim owner templates: agree how to coordinate and whether to divide work or work independently; consider electing a head; explain that `advance` ends the topic and can name the next, and `feedback` rates another participant's behavior for identity/accolades. Describe the head as the normal user of `advance`, not an enforced permission boundary. Verify the actual tool interface before choosing final wording.

Add these requirements and their location to the rules. Keep strategy contributions in the normal discussion loop, with no separate phase. This is proposed implementation work, not a claim that it already happens.

### GF3 — Accept; remove the stale prompt dependency

The builder does not read `seat.limit` while assembling prompts. It reads the limit when submitting a contribution (`src/turn.rs:125–145`). Remove or retire `code.quota.character` as a dependency whose purpose is to tell the participant its current allowance. If the functional map also covers reply resolution, record the enforcement dependency there instead.

The no-characters-line rule concerns the routine discussion allowance banner. It does not prohibit a special topic-proposal request stating its own limit (`src/prompts.rs:85–86`) or a block notice explaining an overlong contribution. Preserve those distinctions.

### GF4 — Partly accept; correct the reviewer's overstatement

The allowance and characters-removed promises are stale: discussion contributions exceeding their limit are blocked before evaluation, not shortened (`src/turn.rs:128–145`). Update the delta-delivery decision and log dependency to say “pending participant notices, including evaluation rejection and overlength blocking,” without promising an allowance or removed-character count.

The description does **not** explicitly promise the objective every turn. The log dependency names topic and objective as available context; the delta-delivery decision names only a changed topic. Reject that portion of the finding as phrased. Still clarify that the configured objective is inserted into the participant template on the first turn (`src/turn.rs:69–78`), while subsequent prompts rely on session continuity. Do not add repeated objective text.

Also avoid the unqualified claim that “truncation no longer exists”: topic proposals are still truncated to `PROPOSAL_LIMIT` in `on_proposal`. The correction applies to discussion contributions.

### GF5 — Accept; document the complete delivery order

Replace the abbreviated ordering rule with the actual assembly sequence (`src/turn.rs:34–68`):

1. Round label, only for a discussion request.
2. First-turn identity profile, only if an identity store and name exist and the stored profile has prior ratings.
3. Pending participant notices, only for a discussion request, in their stored order.
4. Changed-topic line, when topics are enabled, this is not the first prompt, and the participant has not seen the current topic index.
5. Unseen log entries in log order: other participants' accepted messages and chair entries interleaved. Own accepted messages are omitted.
6. Any request-specific `ask`, last.

Parts are separated by blank lines. Notices include overlength blocking and evaluation rejection; include feedback-recording failures in the notice contract as reported by the reviewer, while noting that their `engine.rs:892` producer is outside this snapshot. Do not promise a separate rejection-first sort within the notices: the builder simply extends the stored list. The optional identity profile precedes notices, but the participant's notices still precede other participants' contributions.

### GF6 — Accept; qualify the scope of the rules

The round line and notice consumption are controlled by `discussion`; `ask` is appended independently (`src/turn.rs:34–35,52–54,67,82–92`). Specify that floor turns and workspace-review turns are discussion requests. A review request therefore receives the round line and notices **and** has its review ask last. A topic-proposal, rating, receipt, or results request is a different kind of request and should not be described as receiving discussion notices.

The supplied function establishes the conditional behavior; full verification of how each activity passes `discussion` requires the absent caller. No runtime change is justified by this finding.

### GF7 — Accept; same correction as GF3/GF4

Retire the allowance-reporting dependency and supersede the allowance/removed-characters portions of the delta-delivery decision. Preserve reply-limit enforcement and its explanatory blocking notice. This is the same underlying defect as GF3/GF4, not an additional reason to restore an allowance banner.

Correct stale source documentation too: the `turn_prompt` comment (`src/turn.rs:22–25`), `submit` comment (`src/turn.rs:124`), and module comment (`src/prompts.rs:1–4`) still describe truncation or a characters line. Replace those comments with the actual ordering and block-before-evaluation behavior. Runtime code need not change for this correction.

### GF8 — Accept the ambiguity; do not assume a WORK dependency

Resolve the description conflict as in GF1. `resolve_reply` handles `Reply::Pass`, `Reply::Empty`, and `Reply::Contribution`; it contains no `Reply::Work` branch (`src/turn.rs:97–110`). Work-related state and `after_work` do not prove that the literal text WORK is a required protocol command.

Consequently, the assertion that the engine depends on both literal commands is not established by the supplied code. Document exact recognized syntax and any working-state mechanism in the engine/reply-classification element after inspecting those implementations. Do not introduce a WORK instruction on the strength of this finding.

### GF9 — Accept the documentation gap; distinguish implemented from planned

Put the first-turn kickoff/tool requirements from GF2 in the rules and explicitly label their current implementation status. Do not say that the owner templates already contain them without checking those files.

Chair delivery is implemented: `Entry::Chair` becomes `Chair: text`, interleaved with accepted messages in unseen-log order (`src/turn.rs:60–64`). Document that location. This means the next successfully delivered prompt, potentially a special request, rather than necessarily the next floor turn. The statement that chair guidance bypasses evaluation concerns log admission elsewhere; this builder demonstrates delivery, not that bypass. Preserve it as an upstream contract and verify it at the producer.

### GF10 — Accept; clarify sources and necessary terms

Describe two distinct owner-authored resource inputs, both loaded by `prompts.rs`: `resources/roundtable_prompt.md` is the outer first-turn template; `resources/participant_prompt.md` is the nested participant template, filled with `cfg.objective`. Split the existing system-prompt dependency or enumerate both resources within it; do not invent an unknown functional-map identifier. The current topic comes from `self.topic()`, not from the log traversal. The configured objective also does not come from that traversal.

Define the terms used by this element:

- `R<t>-<m>`: topic index and one-based accepted-message sequence within that topic, **not** discussion round. `accept` constructs it from `j.topic` and accepted log entries (`src/turn.rs`, `accept`).
- `Current delivery:`: the outer template's reported boundary before the rendered delivery. The builder supplies this via `{{delivery_json}}`; despite the placeholder name, its value is plain text joined with blank lines. Confirm the literal marker in the resource.
- Disposition: the participant-facing outcome notice, such as evaluation rejection or overlength blocking.
- JEV: the contribution evaluator; ACP: the participant session protocol whose ongoing conversation supplies continuity.
- Chair: the human/operator supplying guidance; distinct from an elected participant head.
- Accolades: ratings-derived standing associated with a persistent participant identity.
- Work notes: incidental working commentary included in returned participant text. The builder forwards accepted message text as stored; it does not isolate notes from contributions.

These are description improvements. No need to remove the identity profile or rewrite the owner's prompts.

### GF11 — Accept; make topic delivery explicit

Add the exact condition from `src/turn.rs:57–59`: after the first prompt, topics enabled plus an unseen topic index produces `Current topic: …` before log entries. The first-turn wrapper receives the current topic instead. Only the current topic is sent; multiple intervening changes are not replayed as topic history.

Document that committing any delivered prompt updates `seen_topic` and `seen_log`, while only a discussion prompt clears notices (`src/turn.rs:85–92`). A special request can therefore deliver and acknowledge the changed topic before the next floor turn. Preserve this behavior and the first-turn objective/session distinction from GF4.

### GF12 — Accept the wording ambiguity; qualify external claims

Rewrite the round-label rule to state that it chooses **one** label: normally `Round N of T`, replaced near the end by the applicable `3 Rounds Remain`, `2 Rounds Remain`, `1 Round Remains`, or `Final Round`; an unlimited discussion uses `Round N`. They are alternatives, not accumulated suffixes. This records the intended meaning; checking exact boundaries, including short discussions, requires `rules::round_label`, which is absent. The builder only pushes its returned label once (`src/turn.rs:34–35`).

Use the exact topic name `kickoff strategy` for the reported engine-document cross-reference. Correct the referring document if the reported `kickoff` reference exists; that document was not supplied. Neither issue warrants changing prompt assembly.

## Addendum — dissenting/correcting notes (SecureTarget)

Two points where a separate review of the same two files reached a different or sharper
conclusion, recorded so the group can weigh them rather than lose them:

- **GF2 / GF9 (contest the proposed behavioral change).** This resolution proposes adding
  first-turn strategy/tool guidance to the builder's delivery. A separate reading argues against
  implementing it in `turn.rs`: `rules[3]`, the `elephant` "built" line, and the `turn_prompt` doc
  (src/turn.rs:28-30) all state the first turn is *exactly* the owner's roundtable prompt with the
  owner's participant prompt nested inside it, and the `kickoff strategy` decision is explicitly
  tagged `"status": "per owner statements; wording open for owner"` — a proposal, not shipped
  behavior. Adding prose to `turn_prompt` would change the delivered first-turn prompt and
  contradict `rules[3]`. The safer resolution is to mark those `decisions` entries
  unimplemented/superseded and raise "where should this text live" to the owner, as the existing
  `investigations: spec section 11 vs prompt` note already does for owner-authored prompt text.
  It is correct that there is no explicit owner *prohibition* of the text; the objection is to
  changing code on the strength of a stale proposal, not to the text's desirability.

- **GF8 (accept the sharper correction).** The claim that the engine depends on a literal
  first-line **WORK** command is an overstatement. `resolve_reply` (src/turn.rs:97-110) branches on
  `Reply::Pass`, `Reply::Empty`, `Reply::Contribution` only; there is no `Reply::Work` branch, and
  `after_work` is state passed to `submit`, not a parsed control value. The resolution's "do not
  assume a WORK dependency" is the more audit-safe reading and should stand. PASS is genuinely
  parsed (src/turn.rs:99-101, 320-333), so the open question is specifically where *PASS* and the
  working-state mechanism are communicated, not where PASS/WORK are advertised as a pair.

## Resulting scope

Most corrections belong in the description and stale source comments. The proposed behavioral addition is the still-unimplemented first-turn strategy/tool guidance in GF2/GF9, subject to checking the complete templates and tool interface to avoid duplication or inaccurate instructions. Keep the owner templates verbatim, omit routine allowance banners and generic reply directives, and preserve blocking, delta delivery, profile text, and chair/message ordering. Full rendered-prompt storage is another upstream claim: these two files do not establish persistence, so its verification belongs to the discussion-record element.

## QuickCoyote addendum — corrections and the one finding both resolutions get partly wrong

I re-read both source files (`turn.rs`, `prompts.rs`) and the `element.md` text. I agree with the substance of the existing resolutions on GF3, GF5, GF6, GF7, GF10, GF11; I record only where I differ, plus line evidence the earlier passes left implicit.

### GF4 — reject the "objective every turn" half and the "objective appears twice" gap
The reviewers say the description claims the objective "every turn". The description does not: the `wants` entry for `data.log.discussion` says the log *provides* "the current topic and objective" as available context; `turn_prompt` never reads `cfg.objective` except on the first turn (`src/turn.rs:70`, `prompts.rs:12-14`). The delta-delivery decision names only "the topic when it changed". So the Major's first and third clauses are wrong as phrased; only the allowance/"characters removed" clause survives. Note also that the `elephant.gaps` line "objective appears twice on the first turn" is a *known, accepted* duplication — the objective is filled into `{{roundtable_prompt}}` and again into `{{custom_roundtable_prompt}}` via `participant_prompt` (`prompts.rs:70,78`). It is not a finding about delta delivery and should not be "fixed" by deleting either substitution; the owner's template owns that.

### GF8 — "engine depends on PASS/WORK" is not supported; only PASS is parsed
`rules::classify` branches are exercised at `turn.rs:99` (floor) and `turn.rs:320` (proposals), and `resolve_reply` matches `Reply::Pass | Reply::Empty | Reply::Contribution` only (`turn.rs:99-110`); there is no WORK branch in this snapshot. `after_work` is a boolean the caller threads into `submit`, not a parsed verb (`turn.rs:97,147`). So the ambiguity GF8 raises is real (description contradicts rules) but the *premise* ("which the engine depends on") should be narrowed to PASS. Resolution: fix the description conflict (mark the reply-convention decision superseded by the "no instruction to reply" rule); do **not** add a PASS instruction to the prompt without an owner decision, and do not add WORK at all.

### GF2 / GF9 — agree with SecureTarget's dissent, sharpen the reason
Adding kickoff/tool prose inside `turn_prompt` would break three independent statements of invariant: `rules[3]` ("The first turn is the owner's roundtable prompt with the owner's participant prompt inside it and the first turn after 'Current delivery:'"), the `elephant.built` line (`built`), and the doc comment at `src/turn.rs:28-30`. The only place builder text can legally go without touching that invariant is the `delivery` slot (the part after `Current delivery:`), which `roundtable_prompt` fills last (`prompts.rs:79-82`). If the owner wants the kickoff ask, that is the insertion point — and it must be raised to the owner because the kickoff decision is tagged `"wording open for owner"`. My verdict: mark GF2's implementation as *unresolved pending owner wording*, not "add to delivery now". The decision is right that the capability is missing; the code change is premature.

### GF3 — the dependency is real but belongs to reply resolution, not this element
`seat.limit` is read at `turn.rs:126` and enforced at `turn.rs:130`. The `code.quota.character` want in *this* element is wrong because `turn_prompt` never reads it. The clean fix is to move the dependency to the element that owns `submit`, or to rename it "reply length limit (enforced on submit)" and drop "reports the allowance". Do not delete the limitation from the map: the block notice (`prompts::too_long`, `turn.rs:131`) is a participant-facing disposition that this element *delivers* but does not *produce* — which is exactly why the notice contract needs a producer reference.

### GF5 note on ordering within notices
The rules abbreviated order is incomplete, correct. But note the finer point: notices are appended in *arrival* order (`seat.notices.push` at `turn.rs:131`, `216`; cleared only on commit at `turn.rs:89`), so a rejection from a past round can follow a too-long notice from a later one. The rule should say "in the order they arose", not "rejection reasons, then …", or a reader will expect rejection-first sorting that the code does not perform. This is a documentation fix only.

### GF12 — one correction the earlier passes did not make explicit
`round_label` is called once and pushed once (`turn.rs:34-35`); `self.rounds`/`round_no` are supplied by `rules`. The description's phrase "Round N of T, then '3 Rounds Remain'" reads as concatenation because of the word "then"; the rule should state that exactly one label is produced. This is a description fix, no code change; the boundary table (when T=3,4) lives in `rules::round_label` and is out of scope here.

### Scope verdict
Of the twelve findings: GF1, GF5, GF6, GF9, GF10, GF11, GF12 are right and are description fixes. GF3 is right about this element but the fix is to relocate the dependency, not delete enforcement. GF4 is half-right (allowance clause only) and misphrases the objective clause. GF7 is right as a staleness consequence of GF3/GF4 and needs no separate change beyond those. GF2 is right that the capability is missing but wrong to imply a code fix is ready. GF8 is right about the contradiction but overstates the WORK dependency. No finding justifies new prompt code without an owner decision, except the already-open "where does kickoff text live" question.

event.package: event bus library (reusable; basis for the chassis)

owner_statements.statement: We are building two things here: an ACP system that must be reusable by the chassis, with the ACP autoselection and an event bus. Never poll what can surface as an event. What we do here will be used as a basis for the chassis, but this is a standalone tool.

rules: Never poll what can surface as an event: state changes, ACP updates, activity observations, chair commands and JEV results are all published as events.
The bus has no dependency on Roundtable, so the chassis can adopt it unchanged.

decisions.decision: Typed in-process bus. Each subscriber has its own unbounded queue, so publishing never blocks and nothing is dropped; a global sequence number assigned under the same lock as enqueueing gives every subscriber one consistent order. Taps receive every event as an Envelope with lazy JSON, for the discussion record and the GUI. Built on futures channels, with no async-runtime dependency, so the chassis can bridge it into Bevy.
decisions.tradeoff: A subscriber that never reads holds its backlog in memory until dropped. Chosen over bounded or lossy channels because blocking a publisher or losing an event would break never-halt or the complete record.

covers: typed delivery only of own type, in order
tap sees all types in global order, JSON and downcast
publishing never blocks on unread or dropped subscribers; unread subscriber loses nothing (10,000 events)
4 concurrent publishers produce one identical order for two taps

event.name: event bus

elephant.design: Carry every Roundtable event in one order without polling, as the basis of the chassis's event bus.
sources: owner, 2026-11-05: "never poll what can surface as an event"
elephant.built: crates/bus gives every event one global sequence number; every subscriber sees every event in that order; publishing never blocks.
gaps: No stored log or replay: a subscriber that joins late misses earlier events.

findings.finding: Says every subscriber sees every event; a typed Subscription<E> receives only type E (crates/bus/src/lib.rs:138-141, 149-155; tests/bus.rs:22-36). Only Tap receives all events (lib.rs:142-145).

Chair commands are not delivered on the bus: they use a tokio mpsc Command channel (crates/roundtable/src/engine.rs:33-46, 199, 268, 447-451). JEV results return via the Internal mpsc (engine.rs:134-139; turn.rs:177-180). Only their effects are published.
Event-name uniqueness is enforced only by debug_assert! (lib.rs:135-136); release builds silently accept two types under one NAME, making records ambiguous. Undocumented.

Undocumented: Event trait and bounds (lib.rs:34-36), Delivery (lib.rs:94-99), Envelope seq/at/name/to_json/downcast (lib.rs:39-66), recv()/Stream on both receivers, streams end only when every Bus clone drops (lib.rs:166, 194), seq starts at 1, dropped receivers pruned on publish (lib.rs:140, 144).
publish takes the registry mutex (lib.rs:132), so it can wait briefly on other publishers or subscribe calls; poisoned locks are recovered silently.
A failed serialization is cached as None and re-attempted on every to_json call (lib.rs:55-59), so 'serialized once' holds only on success.
'Every subscriber sees every event' contradicts typed delivery of only the subscriber's own type; per the decision, only taps see everything.
The chassis justifies the whole design (no Roundtable dependency, no runtime, Bevy bridge) but is never defined.
ACP, ACP autoselection, JEV, chair commands, never-halt, and Integration Design §6 are used without definition or summary.
Tap vs subscriber and Envelope are undefined; it is not said how a tap is created or whether it is typed.
Late subscribers miss events, but the document doesn't say whether the discussion-record tap is guaranteed to attach before the first event.
Map fields role SE, name_length and the Intent values are undefined.

paraphrase.egm-codebase-details: A reusable in-process event bus (crates/bus) with no Roundtable dependency, built on futures unbounded channels. Every published event gets a global sequence number under one lock. Typed subscriptions receive only their own event type, and taps receive every event as an Envelope with lazily serialized JSON. Publishing never waits on subscribers, and late subscribers miss earlier events.
paraphrase.egm-comprehension: A reusable, typed, in-process event bus with no Roundtable dependency, meant to be adopted unchanged by a later 'chassis'. Publishing never blocks; each subscriber has an unbounded queue, and one global sequence number orders all events. Taps receive every event as an Envelope for the discussion record and GUI. There is no replay, so late subscribers miss earlier events.

# Event bus review resolutions

Author: LethalCohort

Scope: decisions from `element.md` and the supplied `source/crates/bus/src/lib.rs`. This resolves all twelve findings; it does not implement the proposed changes. The snapshot contains no engine, turn module, test source, or Cargo manifest. References to those files in the review are evidence reported by the reviewer, not independently verified here. The description's historical test results have not been rerun.

## GF1 — Accept: correct the description

`subscribe::<E>()` registers by `TypeId` (lib.rs:149–154), and `publish` sends only to the matching typed registry entry (138–141). Taps receive every published type (142–145).

Replace `elephant.built` with: “Each bus instance assigns publications a global sequence number. A typed subscription receives subsequent events of its own type in that order; a tap receives subsequent events of every type in that order. Publication does not wait for consumers to read.” Bus clones share the same instance and sequence; independently constructed buses do not. Typed subscriptions can have gaps in sequence numbers. Retain type filtering in the code: it is intentional and matches the decision. Every-event coverage also requires a receiver to have registered before publication; there is no replay.

The same overstatement must also be corrected in the crate's own module-level rustdoc at **lib.rs:10–11**: “every subscriber receives events in sequence order, whatever their type.” That sentence is the literal origin of the GF1/GF7 wording and would mislead anyone reading the crate source directly. Rewrite it to: “Every event gets a sequence number; a typed subscriber receives its own event type in that order, and a tap receives every type in that order.” This is a rustdoc edit alongside the `element.md` edit, so the fix is consistent at both the crate and the map.

## GF2 — Accept the scope problem; integration details remain unverified

The library can transport any type implementing `Event`. That capability does not establish that chair commands or JEV results actually pass through it. Neither the cited engine/turn code nor integration tests are supplied, so the specific mpsc routes cannot be independently confirmed from this snapshot.

Change the description now to distinguish the owner's event-driven requirement from verified bus adoption. Narrow the manager's current integration claim to verified traffic, and explicitly record chair-command and JEV-result routing as requiring integration verification. If the cited routes are confirmed, record them as a gap against rule 0, which expressly requires those messages to be published as events. An awaited mpsc channel satisfies the no-polling principle, but does not by itself satisfy that stronger bus-publication rule. Publishing only effects is not proof of publishing the command or result itself.

To fulfill the stronger rule, the engine/turn integration must publish command and evaluation-result events and consume them through subscriptions, with an explicit single handler where these represent commands; alternatively, retain direct request channels and publish their receipt/results for observers if the owner clarifies that the bus requirement concerns observability. Verify ordering and exactly-once command execution at that boundary. No change to this generic bus is demonstrated as necessary. Do not silently weaken the owner's rule merely to describe existing routing.

## GF3 — Accept: enforce name uniqueness in release builds

At lib.rs:135–136 the registry remembers the first type for a name, but only `debug_assert!` checks subsequent publications. Release builds can emit indistinguishable names for different payload types. Typed delivery remains correct because it uses `TypeId`; records identified by name become ambiguous. The uniqueness instruction exists in the `Event` rustdoc, but release behavior is not explained.

Use an unconditional assertion for the existing infallible `publish` API, before incrementing the sequence or enqueueing anything. Document that publishing a second type with an already-used name on the same bus panics. Keep the first name-to-type mapping intact. This is a programmer contract violation, not an event to enqueue under an ambiguous name. A fallible publication API could be a separate API decision, but is not needed to correct this defect. The registry can enforce uniqueness only within one bus instance, not across the entire program.

Validate with two distinct types sharing one name under both debug and release builds, and verify that the conflicting payload reaches no receiver. Also cover repeated publication of the same type/name.

**Cross-finding interaction with GF5:** the panic in the GF3 fix fires *while holding the registry `Mutex`*, which is acquired at lib.rs:132 before the name check at 135–136. A panic under `std::sync::Mutex` poisons the lock, so every later `publish`/`subscribe`/`tap` (lines 132, 152, 160) will hit `unwrap_or_else(|poisoned| poisoned.into_inner())` and silently drop the poison — the exact silent-recovery behavior GF5 documents. Thus, after one conflicting-name panic, the registry stays poisoned and the bus keeps running, masking the failure. Two consistent resolutions: (a) place the unconditional uniqueness check *before* any registry mutation (before the `seq` increment and before enqueueing) and keep the GF5 `into_inner()` recovery — the panic then aborts before the registry is changed, so recovery is safe and no ambiguous event is enqueued; or (b) report the conflict without panicking under the lock (e.g. a fallible API). Option (a) is the minimal fix and matches the resolution's "before incrementing the sequence" guidance, but the resolution must state that the panic is expected to poison the lock and that recovery is the designed handling rather than a silent side effect.

## GF4 — Partly accept: add a compact API contract to the map

The map omits useful API details, but “undocumented” overstates the problem: the source already documents the trait, envelope fields, delivery type, receiver lifetime, and several method contracts. This is a discoverability gap in the description, not a missing implementation. Add an API summary with a link to the crate rustdoc:

- `Event: Any + Send + Sync + Debug + Serialize` requires a stable `NAME`; `Any` implies a `'static` event type. Describe the uniqueness enforcement selected in GF3.
- `Bus::new()`/`Default` make independent buses; cloning shares the registry. `publish(E)` returns a sequence number, starting at 1 per instance.
- `subscribe::<E>()` returns `Subscription<E>` yielding `Delivery<E> { seq, at, event: Arc<E> }`. `tap()` returns an untyped `Tap` yielding `Envelope` for every type.
- An envelope exposes `seq`, `at: SystemTime`, and `name`; `downcast::<E>()` returns `Option<&E>`, and `to_json()` is fallible and lazy. State the corrected caching contract from GF6.
- Both receiver types implement `futures::Stream` and asynchronous `recv()`. Registration takes effect under the same registry mutex as publication. Concurrent registration/publication is ordered by lock acquisition.
- Receivers deliver queued items before returning `None` after the last bus clone drops. An idle live bus does not terminate its streams. Dropping a receiver discards its unread queue; its sender is pruned when a later relevant publication attempts delivery. A typed sender may remain registered until its type is published again.

The timestamp is sampled before acquiring the mutex (127–132), so sequence number, rather than wall-clock timestamp, defines publication order. No separate API implementation change is needed for GF4.

## GF5 — Accept the qualification; retain the mutex design

`publish`, `subscribe`, and `tap` use a blocking `std::sync::Mutex` (132, 152, 160). Therefore “publishing never blocks” is too broad. Unbounded queues eliminate waiting for receiver capacity or consumption; they do not make publication lock-free or give it a latency bound. Lock duration includes delivery to all relevant queues and grows with fan-out, so even “briefly” is not a guarantee.

Replace the unconditional wording in the decision, `elephant.built`, and crate-level rustdoc with: “Publication does not wait for subscribers to read or free queue capacity. Publication and registration serialize under a shared mutex.” Preserve the mutex because it orders numbering and enqueueing consistently.

Document the existing poison policy: a poisoned registry lock is recovered with `into_inner()`, without reporting the poison. Recovery is not rollback and does not establish that a panicking publication reached all receivers. This finding alone does not justify changing that policy, but delivery guarantees should be stated for normal successful operation.

## GF6 — Accept: fix failed-serialization caching

The decision's “lazy JSON” is accurate, but `Envelope::to_json` rustdoc promises serialization once per event (52–53), which is false on failure. The first call initializes the cache with `None` after a failed attempt, then immediately calls the serializer again (55–58). Every later call serializes again. For an always-failing serializer, N completed calls therefore make N+1 serialization attempts, not N. Even if a later attempt succeeds, that success is never cached because the `OnceLock` is already initialized to `None`.

Cache the first outcome, success or failure, in the shared once cell and return that outcome on subsequent calls. Keep `to_json()` fallible. Since `serde_json::Error` is not directly cloneable, the implementation must deliberately choose a shareable error representation or reconstruct an appropriate public error; do not propose simply cloning `Result<Value, serde_json::Error>`. Document any loss of error detail if reconstruction is chosen. This preserves lazy, shared, one-attempt serialization and avoids repeated work across taps for malformed payloads.

Validate with a custom failing `Serialize` implementation and a call counter: repeated and concurrent calls through cloned envelopes must invoke serialization once and return errors. Retain a success-cache test. This is a serialization-path fix, not a change to typed event delivery.

## GF7 — Accept; duplicate of GF1

The contradiction is real for the same reasons as GF1. Apply GF1's replacement once, and record GF7 as resolved by that same change. Do not change typed subscribers to receive unrelated types or count this as a second independent implementation defect.

## GF8 — Accept as a context gap, not an established major code defect

The description repeatedly uses the chassis to motivate portability without explaining the term. Add: “The chassis is the intended future host for these reusable components. This bus is designed to be adopted there without Roundtable-specific dependencies.” Describe the Bevy bridge as intended integration, not functionality implemented by this file. The implementation uses futures channels and has no explicit async-runtime API dependency; a complete dependency audit would also need the missing manifest.

No chassis implementation or Bevy bridge should be invented to resolve a terminology finding. Link to the authoritative chassis description if available; the local evidence does not establish further chassis requirements.

## GF9 — Accept: define local terms and summarize the referenced requirement

Add a short glossary: ACP means Agent Client Protocol; ACP autoselection means choosing an ACP implementation automatically; chair commands are control instructions to the discussion coordinator; JEV results are the message evaluator's returned judgments; “never-halt” here means a slow or unread receiver must not force publishers to wait for it. Confirm project-specific expansions and autoselection behavior against authoritative documentation before claiming more detail. The supplied material does not establish the expansion of JEV, so do not invent one.

Summarize the requirement attributed to Integration Design §6 in the map itself: event-driven state propagation and ordered event delivery, using the independently supported local owner statement and decision. Explicitly mark the external section as unavailable for verification here, rather than claiming this summary reproduces its contents. Add a resolvable link when that document is available. Preserve the owner's quotation; explain terms alongside it instead of rewriting historical statements. No code change follows from unexplained terminology.

## GF10 — Accept as a map clarification

Define “subscriber” as the general receiver category. A typed subscription is created by `Bus::subscribe::<E>()` and yields that event type wrapped in `Delivery<E>`. A tap is created by `Bus::tap()` and is untyped: it yields every subsequent published event as an `Envelope`, which carries ordering/time/name metadata and a shared payload accessible through JSON or a checked downcast.

These distinctions already appear in crate rustdoc (15–16, 123, 149, 157); copy the concise contract into the description or refer to GF4's API summary. No new tap API is required.

## GF11 — Accept the missing startup contract; actual loss is unproven

The library supplies no replay and gives no priority to a recording tap. A tap created after an event is published cannot recover it (157–162). The recorder startup path is absent, so neither an existing guarantee nor an actual startup-loss defect can be established here.

Add: “A complete record requires the recording tap to be registered before any event producers start. Its startup ordering is not verified in this snapshot.” If a complete session record is required, the integrating startup code must create the tap synchronously before exposing bus clones to producers, retain it throughout the session, and drain its backlog during shutdown. Add an integration check that the first session event reaches the recorder. A running recorder task is not required before publication; registration is sufficient because its queue buffers unread events. Replay is not necessary to meet this startup contract.

**Recorder order must be `seq`, not `at`:** because `Envelope::at` is sampled before the mutex while `seq` is assigned under it (lib.rs:129 vs 133–134), two events can have `at` ordered opposite to their `seq` (A4). The discussion record therefore must be keyed by `seq` (the bus's global order), never sorted by `at`; otherwise two near-simultaneous publications can appear reordered in the record. Make this explicit in the GF11 startup contract and add an integration assertion that record order equals `seq` order.

## GF12 — Accept as a schema-documentation gap; do not guess schema meanings

The supplied map does not define `role: SE`, `name_length`, or the intent enumeration. Link the shared functional-map schema and give brief field definitions there or beside the properties. Keep `SE` unexpanded until the schema establishes its meaning; likewise, do not declare that `name_length` counts words just because the current name has two words.

The local arrows do establish perspective for these wants: `send` means the named consumer supplies events to the bus, and `send_receive` means it both supplies and consumes them. Document that perspective, then confirm the formal intent enumeration against the schema. This affects reader comprehension, not bus behavior; it requires no code change.

## Disposition

The demonstrated behavioral fixes are release-build name validation (GF3) and one-attempt serialization caching (GF6). GF1/GF7 and GF5 require precise delivery and blocking language. GF4 and GF8–GF12 require API/context documentation and, for GF11, an explicit integration precondition. GF2 needs an honest description of the evidence gap and integration reconciliation against the owner's rule. Missing source prevents claiming the external routing and recorder startup questions are already verified or fixed.

## Addendum — second review (DreadedWisdom)

Full independent analysis and a citation audit are in `DreadedWisdom-decisions.md`. Every `lib.rs`
line reference in GF1, GF3, GF4, GF5, GF6 and GF10 was checked and is accurate; GF1's `tests/bus.rs`
citation and all of GF2's `engine.rs`/`turn.rs` citations are unverifiable because the snapshot
contains only `source/crates/bus/src/lib.rs`. GF2 is the only finding whose entire factual basis
lies outside the supplied source.

Four corrections to the resolutions above:

1. **GF2 — narrow, do not accept as a bus finding.** The element is explicitly a reusable,
   Roundtable-independent library (`rules[1]`, owner statement "standalone tool", `package`
   "reusable"). A bus that carried chair-command or JEV types would violate that rule; the bus
   transports arbitrary `Event` types, and routing is a producer decision in `engine.rs`. This
   document already concedes no generic bus change is necessary, so accepting GF2 as a Blocker on
   this part mislabels a consumer wiring question. The engine redesign ("publish command and
   evaluation-result events and consume them through subscriptions", verify ordering and
   exactly-once execution) belongs in the `code.manager.chat.group`/engine element's findings,
   not here. An awaited mpsc channel is not polling, so the owner's "never poll" principle may
   already hold. For this element: add one scoping sentence to `rules[0]` and to that want — the
   bus is *capable* of carrying these as events; whether a producer publishes them is that
   producer's concern — and record GF2 as forwarded with evidence unverified. Preserve the owner's
   quotation and `rules[0]`; do not weaken them, and do not import an engine redesign here.

2. **GF1/GF7 — the code's own rustdoc has the same defect.** `lib.rs:10–11` says "**One global
   order.** Every event gets a sequence number, and every subscriber receives events in sequence
   order, whatever their type." "whatever their type" reads as a subscriber receiving all types.
   Rewording only `element.md` leaves the contradiction alive in the crate documentation. Add a
   one-line rustdoc fix: "Every event gets one global sequence number. A typed subscription sees
   its own events in that order; a tap sees all events in that order." This is the concrete missing
   step for GF1/GF7.

3. **GF3 — make the pre-mutation placement explicit as a GF5 interaction.** A panic while holding
   the registry `Mutex` poisons it, and `publish` recovers poison silently via `into_inner()`
   (132, also 152 and 160). If the unconditional assertion fired after `registry.seq += 1` (133),
   the recovered registry would skip a sequence number and some queues would be missing an event
   with no signal. Checking uniqueness *before* the increment and before any enqueueing leaves the
   registry untouched. State this reason, not just the placement. Note also that a panic is not
   backpressure, so it does not violate "publishing never blocks".

4. **Group the editorial fixes.** GF4, GF8, GF9, GF10 and GF12 are all "the map uses undefined
   terms / has no API summary" findings and are best resolved by one edit: a "Terms & external
   references" glossary plus a compact "API & semantics" section. Treating them as five separate
   edits invites a repetitive `element.md`. GF12 in particular is a *schema* field set
   (`role`, `name_length`, `Intent`); its definition belongs in the shared functional-map schema,
   not duplicated per element — link it there. GF11's fix is a description note about tap
   registration ordering; adding replay would contradict `elephant.gaps` ("No stored log or
   replay") and the `decisions` memory tradeoff, so replay should not be proposed.

Net effect on disposition: GF3 is the only change that alters runtime behavior in all builds; GF6
is either an optional serialization-cache fix or a rustdoc reword (the `decisions` "lazy JSON" phrasing
is itself accurate, so the finding's cited target is wrong); everything else is description or
single-line rustdoc wording.

## Round 2 additions (RagingTyphon) — corrections to the resolution above

These are verified against `source/crates/bus/src/lib.rs`; they amend, not replace, the decisions above.

### A1. GF5: the lock is released before anyone waits on a receiver — "never blocks" is closer to true than the resolution says

The GF5 section says lock duration "includes delivery to all relevant queues and grows with fan-out," which reads as if the lock is held while a queue operation could wait. It is not: both sends are `unbounded_send` (lib.rs:140, 144), and `futures` `unbounded_send` on an unbounded channel neither yields nor blocks — it only returns `Err` on a disconnected receiver, which `retain` then prunes. So the real inverse of "never blocks" is *memory*, not latency: an unread receiver grows its backlog without bound until dropped (the decision's own tradeoff). Keep the resolution's recommended reword ("does not wait for subscribers to read or free queue capacity"), but drop "grows with fan-out" as a latency claim; the honest statement is that the mutex is held for O(subscribers) non-blocking enqueues plus clones, and publication is not lock-free.

### A2. GF5/poison: `into_inner()` recovery actually violates the ordering guarantee the mutex exists for

`publish` computes `registry.seq += 1` under the lock (133). If a thread panics inside the critical section (e.g. the GF3 `debug_assert!` firing, or an allocation aborting mid-`retain`), the lock is poisoned and the next publisher recovers with `into_inner()` (132) and continues numbering. That is fine for the counter, but the admitted reason for the mutex is "numbering and enqueueing together, so ... every queue receives events in sequence order" (130–131). A panic between assigning `seq` and finishing the `retain` loops (140–144) can leave one queue with seq N-1 and another without it yet, and the recovered publisher then hands out N+1 — so "one consistent order" survives only if panic-in-`publish` cannot happen. Two options, pick one deliberately: (i) keep recovery but document that delivery/ordering guarantees hold only for `publish` calls that do not panic, or (ii) treat a poisoned registry as fatal. Either way this belongs in the map's GF5 note; silence is the only wrong answer.

### A3. GF3: promoting to an unconditional assert panics *while holding* the mutex and *after* the sequence was already consumed

The GF3 fix ("unconditional assertion ... before incrementing the sequence or enqueueing anything") is the right direction, but as written the check in the current code sits *after* `seq += 1` (133–136). The corrected order must be: (1) look up the name→type map; (2) if it conflicts, release without touching `seq`, then panic (or return an error from a fallible API) — i.e. the conflict check precedes the increment and precedes any `retain`. This also avoids the A2 poisoning path for the one panic that GF3 will deliberately introduce. A `HashMap<&'static str, TypeId>` probe that has to `entry(...).or_insert` does the insert as a side effect; restructure to probe first, insert the mapping only after the conflict check passes, so a rejected publication leaves the registry unchanged (the existing "keep the first name-to-type mapping intact" note in GF3 already wants this — this makes it literal).

### A4. GF4: one API fact is missing and one is mis-stated

- Missing: `Envelope::downcast` (`lib.rs:63–65`) only returns the payload when the envelope's concrete type is `E`; a tap that downcasts to the wrong type gets `None`, silently. Combined with GF3's release-build name ambiguity (two types, one `NAME`), a tap that keys on `name` and downcasts to the expected type can also get `None` — worth one line in the map so readers do not assume `name` ⇒ successful `downcast`.
- Mis-stated: the resolution's GF4 bullet "Concurrent registration/publication is ordered by lock acquisition" is true, but the sequence number is assigned under that lock (133–134) while `at` is sampled *before* it (129). Two publishers that sample `at` in one order can receive sequence numbers in the opposite order. The resolution already notes "sequence number, rather than wall-clock timestamp, defines publication order" — good; but it should also warn that `at` is not monotonic with `seq`, so any recorder that sorts by `at` can reorder relative to `seq`.

### Net effect on the disposition

Unchanged: GF3 and GF6 remain the behavioral fixes; GF1/GF7/GF5 are wording; GF4/GF8–GF12 are documentation; GF2 is unverifiable here. What changes is the *substance* of two of them — GF3's assertion must move before the `seq` increment (A3), and GF5 must stop implying lock-held-while-waiting and instead state the memory/poison caveats (A1, A2).

## Round 2, part 2 (DreadedWisdom) — agreement, one sharpening, one unresolved disagreement

I checked A1–A4 against the code and agree with all four. Two additions:

**A2/A3 sharpening: the poisoning path is already live, not hypothetical.** The current
`debug_assert!(known == TypeId::of::<E>())` at `lib.rs:136` fires **in debug builds while the
registry mutex is held**, and it already sits *after* `registry.seq += 1` (133). So a duplicate
`NAME` in a debug build today panics mid-critical-section, poisons the lock, and the next
`publish` recovers via `into_inner()` (132) from a registry that has already consumed a sequence
number. The GF3 fix does not *introduce* this risk; it makes it deterministic in release builds
too. That is the strongest argument for A3's ordering (probe the name map first, insert the
mapping only after the conflict check passes, increment `seq` last) and for A2's "guarantees hold
only for non-panicking publishes" note. Also note the two error paths differ: `Envelope::to_json`
(GF6) runs on a receiver, outside the lock, so a serialization failure can never poison the
registry — only `publish` can.

**A1 clarification, not a correction.** LethalCohort's "lock duration grows with fan-out" is a
true statement about *hold time* (O(subscribers) clones plus `unbounded_send` calls, 139–144),
not a claim that a queue operation waits. RagingTyphon's "drop it as a latency claim" is right
only if a reader mistakes hold time for backpressure. The accurate merge of both is: the mutex is
held for O(subscribers) non-blocking enqueues; publication is not lock-free and has no latency
bound, but never waits on receiver capacity or consumption. My own GF5 wording in the addendum
above is consistent with this.

**Unresolved: GF2.** RagingTyphon's additions address GF3/GF4/GF5 but leave GF2 as "unverifiable
here" while the main resolution still "accepts the scope problem" and prescribes engine-side
redesign. My position stands: GF2 is **not a finding against the event bus element** and should
not be recorded as an accepted Blocker on this part. The bus is deliberately Roundtable-
independent (`rules[1]`, owner statement, `package`); it has no chair-command or JEV types by
design and carries arbitrary `Event` types. The document already concedes no generic bus change
is needed, so the correct resolution for *this* element is (a) one scoping sentence in `rules[0]`
and the `code.manager.chat.group` want — the bus provides the capability, producer wiring is the
producer's concern — and (b) forward GF2, with its unverified evidence, to the engine/chat.group
element. Preserve the owner's quotation and `rules[0]`; do not weaken them and do not carry an
engine redesign in this document. This is the one decision the group should still settle.

**Still unclaimed: the `lib.rs:10–11` rustdoc fix (GF1/GF7).** Neither addendum picks up the
crate-level "every subscriber receives events in sequence order, whatever their type" line. Until
that one line is reworded, the contradiction GF1 and GF7 identify survives in the code's own
documentation even after `element.md` is corrected. It is a single-line change and belongs in the
final edit list.

**Editorial grouping (addendum point 4) also still stands:** GF4, GF8, GF9, GF10 and GF12 are one
glossary + API-section edit, with GF12's schema fields defined in the shared map schema rather
than duplicated here.
