# OpenRouter review resolutions

Prepared by GhostShade from `element.md` and the supplied source snapshot. These are decisions and proposed changes; no source changes are made. Source paths below are relative to `source/`.

Three source files were supplied in this element's `source/`: the two catalog readers and `jev.rs`. The sibling element `code.adapter.agent` additionally ships `adapter.ts` and `tools.ts` at `../code.adapter.agent/source/adapters/openrouter-acp/src/` (verified present), so GF1/GF5 claims citing those two files ARE re-verifiable from the workspace. Only `tables.rs` is absent from all copies, and only claims about historical runs lack evidence. The evidence inventory is in `GhostShade-evidence.md`.

# Merge addendum (UnifiedRazor, second/third rounds)

The header caveat in the merged draft ("`adapter.ts`/`tools.ts` cannot be re-verified") is outdated. They are in this workspace: the sibling element `code.adapter.agent` ships them at `../code.adapter.agent/source/adapters/openrouter-acp/src/` (verified: `adapter.ts`, `tools.ts`, `models.ts`, etc.). Verified directly there:
- `adapter.ts:127-136` — throws `authRequired` / "OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not set in the environment of the openrouter-acp adapter process" (was GF5, adapter half — now confirmed);
- `tools.ts:34` — `WITHHELD_ENV = ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]`, stripped at `:256-257` before spawning `/bin/sh` (GF5, key-withholding — now confirmed);
- `adapter.ts:226-231` — `retryConfig: { strategy: "none" }` (new confirmed fact: the adapter does not retry).
Only `tables.rs` is in neither this copy nor the sibling's, so only its two citations (GF2 `:76-79`, GF5 `:68-70`) keep the "needs confirmation" flag. The scope note (line 5) and GF5 (line 58) have since been corrected to reflect that `adapter.ts`/`tools.ts` ARE verifiable; `GhostShade-evidence.md:12` still lists them as "not supplied" and is the one remaining stale artifact — it should be read as describing only this element's `source/`, not the whole workspace.

## GF4 consequence added (fail-open)
Per `jev.rs:1-3` ("the caller shares the contribution unjudged on error"), the `Err("no OpenRouter key configured")` at `jev.rs:153` silently disables JEV's veto rather than aborting the round. The description should record this fail-open consequence of a missing key, not just the missing call.

## GF9 rejection
Corroborated from two directions: the sibling element's own report that the adapter is listed first in the harness catalog, and `models.ts:3-5` ("every time a session is created"). "Rarely used" has no telemetry support; per-session selectability is the verifiable statement.

## GF1 — Accept the endpoint correction; change the description

The adapter catalog explicitly identifies the Agent SDK's endpoint as `/api/v1/responses` and admits models only when their advertised endpoints include that value (`adapters/openrouter-acp/src/models.ts:19–20,64–68`). Describing this as “chat completions” is ambiguous and can incorrectly imply the Chat Completions API. The actual SDK invocation cited by the reviewer is absent from this snapshot, but the supplied endpoint contract supports the correction.

Replace the adapter want's function with: **“Runs inference for the selected published OpenRouter model identifier; the openrouter-acp Agent SDK integration uses the Responses API (`POST /api/v1/responses`).”** Keep other adapter implementations' routes separate unless verified. Do not switch the code to Chat Completions to match the wording: no requirement or defect justifies that change. The mismatch is in the description, rather than proof that inference is unimplemented.

## GF2 — Accept the missing integration; qualify the ordering claim

The built account names the catalog, OpenCode seats, and JEV, but omits openrouter-acp. Its supplied catalog implementation provides direct evidence of that integration. Add **“the openrouter-acp integration, which obtains session model options from OpenRouter and selects models compatible with tools and Responses”** to `elephant.built`.

The assertion that this adapter is offered first depends on the missing `crates/roundtable-web/src/tables.rs`; it is not independently established. Ordering is not needed to correct the omission and should not be added as an enduring service responsibility. No source change is warranted by the omission alone.

## GF3 — Accept; describe both catalog consumers and their different contracts

Both readers call `GET https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models`, but their outputs and request behavior differ:

| Consumer | Supplied behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/acp-host/src/models.rs:8–29` | Makes one request, adds bearer authorization only when passed a key, and returns `id`, `name`, and optional `context_length`. No pagination or capability filter is implemented. |
| `adapters/openrouter-acp/src/models.ts:43–81` | Sends bearer authorization using its required key argument, follows `links.next`, filters for `tools` and `/api/v1/responses`, deduplicates accepted IDs, and returns model value/name choices. Throws when no compatible options remain. |

Expand the catalog description to distinguish the general listing from adapter session choices. Attribute filtering and pagination to the callers, rather than to OpenRouter itself. A published identifier in the host listing is not by itself a guarantee of compatibility with the adapter.

No code change follows automatically: these consumers can legitimately need different lists. If the intended requirement is that the host listing always equals the adapter's runnable choices, that requirement must be made explicit before aligning their implementations. Similarly, the one-request reader is not proven broken without evidence that pagination is required for its use.

## GF4 — Accept; document the separate JEV contract

`crates/roundtable/src/jev.rs:16–18,133–175` establishes the default route `POST https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions`, default model `~typesafe/jev-latest`, bearer authentication, and JSON body `{model, state, questions}`. URL and model are public fields initialized to those defaults, so the description should not call them immutable.

Add this route as a distinct dependency for JEV evaluation. Describe its named numeric answers: `noul` values must be within 0–1, and scores within their question's criteria range. Missing or blank keys prevent an HTTP call and produce an error; HTTP failures, unreadable answers, missing answers, and out-of-range values also produce errors. Label the configured default endpoint as alpha, as its path indicates.

The file's module comment says callers share contributions unjudged on error, but the caller is absent. Attribute that fallback to the caller and verify it there before stating it as observed end-to-end behavior. No JEV implementation change is required by this documentation omission.

## GF5 — Partly supported; accept credential documentation, reserve the specific claims

The supplied code proves that the adapter catalog sends a bearer token (`models.ts:45–52`) and JEV requires a nonblank configured key (`jev.rs:133–155`). The host catalog can request the listing without a key (`models.rs:17–27`). Document these distinctions instead of stating that every OpenRouter operation requires a configured key.

The claim that a seat key arrives only when `share_openrouter_key` is enabled cites `tables.rs`, which is absent from all copies; it remains unverified, not disproved, and should be confirmed before being written as fact. The claims that the adapter reads `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` (`adapter.ts:127-136`, `authRequired`) and removes it from model-run commands (`tools.ts:34`, `WITHHELD_ENV`, applied at `:256-257`) ARE confirmed from the sibling element's source (see merge addendum line 9-12), so they may be documented as verified — subject to verifying that the sibling file matches the deployed adapter build. If confirmed, describe the environment variable, opt-in forwarding, and command-environment filtering as separate responsibilities of the integration. Do not infer broad credential isolation from one environment filter. No source defect is established here.

## GF6 — Accept the missing functional dependency; avoid inventing a consumer boundary

The account says OpenRouter supplies JEV, yet the wants contain only participant inference and catalog retrieval. JEV's concrete dependency is confirmed by `jev.rs:152–175`. Add a want for `upstream.judge.llm` describing authenticated structured decisions over state and named questions, using the contract in GF4.

Also make OpenCode-backed participant inference explicit, consistent with the existing built account, while noting its implementation is not supplied here. If `code.adapter.agent` already encompasses OpenCode seats, expand that want rather than inventing a duplicate map element. These edits explain which consumer needs which operation; they do not require changes to working inference code.

## GF7 — Accept the prerequisite gap; do not treat the run statistic as verified

Add operation-specific credential prerequisites from GF5 and explain that external inference and decisions depend on account funding or allowances and service limits applicable to the chosen route/model. Catalog availability does not demonstrate that a later inference or evaluation request will succeed. Avoid fixed balances, rates, or a universal paid-credit requirement without authoritative evidence.

The alleged “68 HTTP 402 credit errors” in run 1 is not present in the supplied files. Retain it only as a reviewer-reported observation until run logs establish the count, route, response details, and impact. The snapshot shows JEV returning non-success statuses as errors (`jev.rs:158–159`), but does not establish credit exhaustion detection, retry behavior in callers, or the cause of that run's failures. Do not prescribe retries or billing-handling code on that evidence alone. Exact current provider limits would require separate verification.

## GF8 — Partly accept as reference completeness; correct the proposed endpoint

The existing models URI is appropriate for the catalog and is not false merely because it is the sole link. However, the expanded description should provide references for each distinct API dependency: Models, Responses, and the alpha Decisions route. In particular, GF1 establishes that Responses is the relevant adapter API; adding only a Chat Completions reference would perpetuate the mismatch. Retain the canonical models URI if the map schema allows only one property URI and add other references in a supported description/reference section. Verify documentation destinations before inserting them; no new documentation URLs are asserted here. No source change is needed.

## GF9 — Reject as a required correction

Nothing supplied establishes that `code.adapter.agent` is rarely used. Being offered first, even if confirmed, would not establish frequency of use. A wants list describes a dependency's responsibility, not its popularity; a rarely selected integration still needs correct behavior.

Keep the adapter want. If usage frequency becomes relevant to a maintenance decision, record it separately with a time period and telemetry or other evidence. Do not label the adapter rare or remove its contract on the basis of this finding.

## Resulting scope

The supported resolutions require a clearer map description: distinguish catalog consumers, identify Responses-based participant inference, describe JEV's authenticated Decisions API, and record operation-specific prerequisites. The findings do not establish a source defect requiring implementation changes. Claims dependent on omitted files or run logs remain explicitly unverified; no implementation changes or runtime tests were performed for this document-only task.

Roundtable checks each message with one five-question request (three gates and two scores) and compares pairs of proposed topics in one batched request. roundtable.resolution:
# Resolution of review findings for `upstream.judge.llm` (JEV)

Decisions on GF1–GF10. Each finding is judged against the code in `source/` plus the sibling copies of `turn.rs` and `rules.rs` that the findings cite (the same Roundtable crate is copied into each sibling `source/` folder; JEV's own `source/` contains only `crates/roundtable/src/jev.rs`). For each finding: whether it is right, and what should change in the code or the description, with the reason.

Verified code facts used throughout (from `source/crates/roundtable/src/jev.rs` and the cited sibling `turn.rs`/`rules.rs`):

- `jev.rs:42-59`: `contribution_questions()` builds a `BTreeMap` of **five** questions — three `noul` gates named `contribution`, `usefulness`, `relevance` (lines 43-47), then two `score` questions named `value`, `auditability` (lines 50-53). The header comment `jev.rs:5-7` and the test `jev.rs:191-194` confirm five questions, scores with 6 criteria levels, and no criteria on `relevance`.
- `jev.rs:150-175`: `ask()` returns `Result<BTreeMap<String, f64>, String>` — **one number per question name**, no reasons, no text. It reads `reply["answers"][name][question.kind]` as a float (line 168), range-checks `0.0..=top` (lines 165-170), and errors on out-of-range (line 170) or HTTP failure with the body cut to 300 chars (line 159).
- `rules.rs:13,15` (sibling `code.quota.character`): `GATE_PASS = 0.70` for the three yes/no gates and `SCORE_PASS = 3.0` for the two 0-5 scores.
- `turn.rs:204-226` (sibling `code.gate.quality`, `on_judged`): builds `checks` = gates at `GATE_PASS` chained with scores at `SCORE_PASS`, collects every `failed` check as `(name, value)` pairs, and on failure pushes `prompts::rejected(&failed)` to the seat and broadcasts a rejected `Contribution` whose `reasons` are `format!("{name} {value:.2}")`. **The rejection/reason text is assembled by Roundtable, not returned by JEV.**
- `turn.rs:152-167` (sibling): `!jev.configured()` (no key) → shared unjudged (line 152-153); a `contribution_state` error (message cannot fit) → loud `notice("error", ...)` then shared unjudged (lines 160-165). `on_judged` `Err(reason)` → loud notice + shared unjudged (the "JEV unavailable" branch).
- `jev.rs:1-3`: "No timer: it gets a reply or an error."
- `jev.rs:116-123`: `sameness_question` reads `resources/topic_sameness.md` and replaces `{{foo}}`/`{{bar}}` with `proposals.p{a}`/`proposals.p{b}`.
- `turn.rs:352-354` (sibling `code.selector.topic`): pairs batched under names `p{a}_{b}` from `rules::pairs(...)`.
- `jev.rs:62-72, 74-103`: `HISTORY_ROUNDS=4`, `STATE_PLUS_QUESTION_TOKENS=32_000`, `REQUEST_TOKENS=64_000`, `estimate_tokens` = one token per 3 bytes of JSON (`s.len().div_ceil(3)`), state holds `topic`, `conversation` grouped by round, `new_message`, oldest messages dropped first (line 101). `~typesafe/jev-latest` at `jev.rs:18`, decision route URL `jev.rs:16`.

---

## GF1 (Blocker) — RIGHT

The core claim is right and it is a Blocker: the `code.gate.quality` want at `element.md:15` says JEV "Returns a confidence for each of the three contribution conditions, with reasons for any that fall short, in one request." This is false on three counts, all verified in code:

1. There are **five** questions, not three: three `noul` gates plus two `score` questions (`jev.rs:42-59`).
2. `ask()` returns exactly one `f64` per question name and **no reasons of any kind** — the return type is `Result<BTreeMap<String, f64>, String>` (`jev.rs:152`, `162-174`).
3. The rejection text is built by Roundtable in `on_judged` from the failed `(name, value)` pairs (`turn.rs:204-216`), not by JEV. JEV supplies only numbers; the "reasons" are `format!("{name} {value:.2}")` strings that name which check fell below its threshold and its value.

This also contradicts the document's own `elephant` (`element.md:86`, "five checks") — a genuine internal inconsistency. **Consequence:** a caller reading the want would build a client expecting three confidences and human-readable reason strings, and would reject or mis-parse the five-number reply.

The score range is determined by six ordered criteria levels (`0..=levels.len()-1`, hence `0..=5`), independently of the acceptance cutoff of 3.0. Results are read as floating-point numbers; integer-only scores are not enforced.

**What should change — the description (the want), not the code.** The code is correct and self-consistent (five questions, one number each); the description is the stale artifact. Rewrite `element.md:15` (the `code.gate.quality` want's Function) to state that one request carries five questions (three yes/no gates + two 0-5 scores), that JEV returns one confidence/value per named question with **no** reasons, that the three gates pass at 0.70 and the two scores at 3.0, and that Roundtable (the caller) constructs the rejection text from the failing names and values. Also update `element.md:86` elephant "five checks" is consistent once the want is fixed — keep it. Do **not** change the code to add reasons: the owner statement (`element.md:71-74`) says confidence is consumed as a decision value/number, never as a similarity distance, and archaeology (`element.md:48`) describes `answers[name].noul = probability true` with no reason field. Adding model-generated reasons would require a separately specified and verified interface change; the supplied code does not establish whether the provider supports such a field.

## GF2 (Major) — RIGHT

The `references` note (`element.md:29`) says "the current spec specifies three conditions at 0.70." Verified: the code checks **three** gates at `GATE_PASS = 0.70` (`rules.rs:13-15`) **and** **two** scores at `SCORE_PASS = 3.0` used in `on_judged` (`turn.rs:207-210`). So "three conditions at 0.70" is an incomplete description of the pass criteria — it omits the two score thresholds entirely and implies 0.70 applies to all five checks.

This is Major (an important gap), not a Blocker, because the note is about a comparison to run 1's four-score setup at 0.83; the missing score thresholds mislead about how many checks exist and at what level, which feeds directly into the GF1 confusion.

**What should change — the description.** Amend `element.md:29` (and, consistently, the `owner_statements` note at `element.md:68`) to say the current spec sets **three yes/no gates at 0.70 and two 0-5 scores at 3.0**, i.e. five checks total. The owner statement "0.70 is better for this purpose" (`element.md:67`) is specifically about the `code.gate.quality` threshold and is confirmed by `rules.rs:13`; it remains true, but should be annotated that it governs the gates only, with the scores at 3.0. No code change: thresholds are correct in `rules.rs`.

## GF3 (Major) — RIGHT

All four sub-claims are verified in `jev.rs`:
- `score` question type carries ordered `criteria` levels (`jev.rs:20-40`, `score()` splits instructions from one-level-per-line criteria; test `jev.rs:192-193` shows 6 levels).
- State contents: topic, `HISTORY_ROUNDS=4` completed rounds plus current round (comment `jev.rs:61`, `first = round.saturating_sub(4)` at `jev.rs:80`), and `new_message`, oldest dropped first (`jev.rs:101`).
- Two token limits: `STATE_PLUS_QUESTION_TOKENS=32_000` and `REQUEST_TOKENS=64_000` (`jev.rs:64-66`, enforced at `jev.rs:94`).
- Token estimate one per 3 bytes (`jev.rs:68-72`), and out-of-range answers are errors (`jev.rs:163-171`).

None of this is in `element.md`. This is Major: a caller integrating JEV needs the request shape (`{model, state, questions}`), the two question types and their answer ranges, the state schema, the two token budgets, and the estimation rule. Without it, the `investigations` note (`element.md:39`) about "64K input" is the only hint and it does not say 32K applies to state-plus-longest-question or that answers are range-checked.

**What should change — the description.** Add a layer (e.g. extend `archaeology` or add a `contract`/`interface` layer) documenting: request body `{"model","state","questions"}`; question types `noul` (answer 0..1 probability) and `score` (answer 0..last-criteria-level, ordered levels in `criteria`); the five named question set; state fields (`topic`, `conversation` grouped by round of last 4 completed + current round, `new_message`); `HISTORY_ROUNDS=4`, estimated state-plus-longest-question <= 32,000 and estimated state-plus-all-questions <= 64,000; estimate = ceil(JSON UTF-8 bytes / 3); the outer request envelope and model are omitted from that check, so it is not an exact full-body or provider-token guarantee; oldest messages dropped first; out-of-range or missing answers are errors. No code change — the code is correct; the gap is documentation.

## GF4 (Major) — RIGHT

Verified failure behaviour, none of it in `element.md`:
- No key (`!self.jev.configured()`) → shared unjudged, `turn.rs:152-153` (sibling `code.gate.quality`). The finding's cite `turn.rs:152-167` covers this and the "cannot fit" case.
- Message that cannot fit (`contribution_state` `Err`) → `notice("error", ...)` loudly + shared unjudged, `turn.rs:160-165`.
- JEV error (`on_judged` `Err(reason)`) → loud notice + shared unjudged with "JEV unavailable", `turn.rs:199-203` region (the exact notice line in the sibling is just after `on_judged`'s `Err` arm).
- No timer: `jev.rs:3` "No timer: it gets a reply or an error."
- HTTP error bodies cut to 300 chars: `jev.rs:159`.

This is Major: "shared unjudged on failure" is a security/quality-relevant behaviour (a message that bypasses the gate is broadcast to every participant), and a caller must know that this module adds no evaluation timer and that messages exceeding JEV context budgets or producing evaluation errors are shared unjudged. This does not override the separate character-length rejection earlier in the caller. `element.md` currently says nothing about any failure path.

**What should change — the description.** Add a `failure behaviour` note to the element: no key / oversized message / JEV error all result in the contribution being **shared unjudged** (not rejected), errors produce a loud notice, this module adds no evaluation timer (the injected reqwest client may have its own timeout), and HTTP error diagnostics include only the first 300 characters of the response body. The full response body is read before that truncation, so this is not a download-size cap. Note the design consequence: the `code.gate.quality` want's "decide before broadcast whether a contribution is worth every other participant's input tokens" is **best-effort**, not guaranteed — on any of these failures the gate is bypassed. This reconciles the want with reality. No code change.

## GF5 (Nit) — RIGHT, no change required (for the record)

The `code.selector.topic` want (`element.md:16`) says pairs "may be batched in one request" and JEV "judges whether two proposed topics express the same underlying intent and returns a confidence for each pair." Verified accurate: `sameness_question` uses `resources/topic_sameness.md` with `{{foo}}`/`{{bar}}` replaced (`jev.rs:116-123`), and pairs are batched under names `p{a}_{b}` (`code.selector.topic/.../turn.rs:352-354`). This is a "Nit ... For the record" finding — it is an accurate observation, not a defect. **Decision:** right as a factual note; no change to code or description is required. Optionally add the two citations to the want as supporting detail, but this is a Nit and not necessary.

## GF6 (Major) — PARTLY RIGHT

The missing gate names and incomplete current want are real defects. However, three gates plus two scores are compatible with five checks. The owner statements approve the gate cutoff and explain JEV's role; they do not claim that there can only be three checks. The five-question specification is separately attributed to the owner on 7 November in `jev.rs:5–7`. Preserve the dated statements and annotate their scope rather than treating them as contradictory. The three unnamed gates are `contribution`, `usefulness`, and `relevance`; the two scores are `value` and `auditability`.

**What should change — the description.** Name the three gates (`contribution`, `usefulness`, `relevance`) and the two scores (`value`, `auditability`) in the want and/or a new contract layer, and make the count consistent everywhere: five checks per message (three gates + two scores). The elephant's "five checks" is correct; keep it. Reconcile the owner statement (0.70 for this purpose) as gate-specific (see GF2). No code change.

## GF7 (Major) — RIGHT

Verified: `jev.rs:18` uses `~typesafe/jev-latest` ("The owner's choice: always the newest JEV release"), while archaeology (`element.md:48`) records the pinned dated snapshot `typesafe/jev-1.13` (`-20260917`). The `~` prefix and the move off a pinned snapshot are not explained anywhere in `element.md`. "decision route" in the elephant (`element.md:86`) only makes sense as `POST /api/alpha/decisions` via archaeology (`element.md:48`), but that connection is not stated. This is Major: pinning vs. "latest" changes reproducibility — a dated snapshot gives stable behaviour, `~...-latest` means the model behind the gate can change at any time without a code change, which directly affects the "accuracy falls as irrelevant state grows / leans toward first option" weaknesses in archaeology (`element.md:52`) and the unverified operating characteristics.

**What should change — the description.** Add a note to `elephant` / `archaeology`: the current code calls `~typesafe/jev-latest` through `DECISIONS_URL = https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions` (`jev.rs:16`); the code passes the leading `~` verbatim and does not define its meaning. The adjacent comment attributes choosing the newest JEV release to the owner; it does not establish which part of the identifier implements provider routing. Mark provider interpretation of `~` as unverified rather than asserting an undocumented syntax rule. State explicitly that archaeology describes a **dated, earlier snapshot** and that the "decision route" is `/api/alpha/decisions`. Mention that `~...-latest` trades reproducibility for always-current behaviour. No code change (the code is the owner's deliberate choice); the gap is the unexplained drift between the documented archaeology model and the running model.

## GF8 (Major) — RIGHT

Verified as a real open inconsistency in `element.md`:
- `investigations` (`element.md:39`): "~$0.42/M input", owner-supplied, unverified.
- `archaeology` (`element.md:56`): "PRICE CONFLICT: the archive records $0.042 per million input tokens; README 5 says ~$0.42. Unverified." — a 10× discrepancy ($0.042 vs $0.42).
- `elephant` (`element.md:86`): "about $0.00005 per message for five checks" — does not say which price it assumes.

This is Major: a 10× price difference changes the cost estimate that justifies "judges each message cheaply before it reaches the group" (`element.md:82`), and the per-message figure is unreconstructable without knowing the assumed price and token count. `element.md:39` already flags that operating characteristics must be verified against OpenRouter.

**What should change — the description.** In `investigations` and `elephant`, state that the price conflict is **unresolved** and must be verified against OpenRouter before any cost claim is relied on; annotate `$0.00005 per message` with the assumed input price (which of $0.042/M or $0.42/M) and the assumed tokens per message, or mark it as an unverified estimate. Do **not** silently pick one price. No code change — cost is not in the code; this is a documentation/verification item. Optionally add a targeted action: verify the live `~typesafe/jev-latest` input price on OpenRouter and record the result.

## GF9 (Nit) — RIGHT

`archaeology` (`element.md:48`) uses the term `noul` ("each question `{type:'noul', ...}`", "`answers[name].noul = probability true`") without explaining what `noul` means, and the request shape `{model, state, questions}` / `criteria:{true,false}` is given only as a compact literal. Verified from `jev.rs:20-33`: a `noul` question is a yes/no question whose answer is "how sure JEV is that the answer is yes (0 to 1)"; the reply is read at `reply["answers"][name]["noul"]` (`jev.rs:168`). The archaeology's `criteria:{true,false}` is the older/pinned-snapshot shape; the current code uses `criteria: Option<Vec<String>>` only for `score` questions and `None` for `noul` (`jev.rs:27-33`). This is a Nit (terminology/readability), not a defect in behaviour.

**What should change — the description.** Add a one-line gloss to `archaeology`: "`noul` = a yes/no question answered as a probability (0..1) that the answer is yes" and note that the request is `{model, state, questions}` where each question has `type`, `instructions`, and (for `score`) ordered `criteria` levels. Also note the pinned-snapshot `criteria:{true,false}` wording differs from the current `noul` (no criteria) / `score` (ordered string levels) shape, which GF3's new contract layer will spell out. No code change.

## GF10 (Nit) — RIGHT

`element.md:3` says "Paths are relative to the Roundtable folder," but the `references` layer (`element.md:28`) contains `~/topogee/docs/roundtables/1-embodied-ai-in-a-3d-physics/Roundtable_1_First_Run_Analysis_and_Failure_Audit.md` — a home-directory absolute-ish path. This breaks the header's own rule. Verified by inspection of the document itself. Nit severity is appropriate (a documentation-path inconsistency, no behavioural impact).

**What should change — the description.** Either (a) restate the header to say reference paths may be absolute/home-relative while code paths are relative to the Roundtable folder, or (b) relocate/copy the referenced run-1 analysis into the Roundtable folder and use a relative path. Recommendation: **(a)** is lower-effort and honest — the run-1 audit is an external historical artifact, not part of the Roundtable tree, so forcing it into the relative-path convention would misrepresent where it lives. Add a note in the reference entry that it is an external document outside the Roundtable folder. No code change.

---

## Summary table

| Finding | Right? | Severity agreed? | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| GF1 | Right | Blocker | **Description**: rewrite `code.gate.quality` want — five questions, one number each, NO reasons, reasons built by caller; gates 0.70 / scores 3.0. No code change. |
| GF2 | Right | Major | **Description**: note should say three gates at 0.70 AND two scores at 3.0. |
| GF3 | Right | Major | **Description**: document request shape, `noul`/`score` types + ranges, state schema, 32K/64K limits, 1-token/3-byte estimate, range-check errors. |
| GF4 | Right | Major | **Description**: document shared-unjudged failure paths, no timer, 300-char error cut, and that the "before broadcast" gate is best-effort. |
| GF5 | Right (accurate, for the record) | Nit | No change required; optionally add the two citations. |
| GF6 | Partly right | Naming and scope gap accepted | **Description**: name the three gates + two scores; preserve gate-specific owner statements. Three gates plus two scores are compatible with five checks. |
| GF7 | Right | Major | **Description**: explain `~...-latest` vs pinned `jev-1.13`, that the owner intends newest-release selection while provider semantics of `~` remain unverified, and that the "decision route" = `/api/alpha/decisions`. |
| GF8 | Right | Major | **Description**: flag the $0.042 vs $0.42 conflict as unresolved; state the price assumed by $0.00005/message; verify on OpenRouter. |
| GF9 | Right | Nit | **Description**: gloss `noul` = yes/no probability; note current shape differs from the pinned-snapshot `criteria:{true,false}`. |
| GF10 | Right | Nit | **Description**: fix the header rule or mark the run-1 path as external; recommend the latter. |

**Overall:** the description needs corrections for the accepted findings; GF5 confirms existing behavior and GF6 is only partly right because the owner statements do not contradict five checks. The inspected code supports the documented five-check design; the defects are all in `element.md` — stale/incomplete wants, an internal count inconsistency, an unexplained model change, an unresolved price conflict, undocumented contract and failure behaviour, and two nits. No code changes are recommended. The description should be updated and the two open verification items (live model price, `~` semantics) confirmed against OpenRouter.

findings.finding: 'Read at start-up for the harness catalog' is false. autoselect fetches REGISTRY_URL every time it is called (crates/acp-host/src/launch.rs:214-219). It is called on every harness-list request (crates/roundtable-web/src/app.rs:209-210) and at table creation (crates/roundtable-web/src/tables.rs:110-112). Nothing reads it at start-up or caches it.

The launch order is undocumented. A binary already on PATH runs directly with the registry's arguments (launch.rs:117-125). Otherwise `acpr <id>` is used when acpr is installed (launch.rs:96-98, 126-127). Without acpr, npx or uvx entries run directly with a note (launch.rs:128-130), and binary-only entries are unavailable (launch.rs:131-133). The binary is chosen by platform key (launch.rs:140-147).

The security filter is undocumented: entries may not set PATH, NODE_OPTIONS, NODE_PATH, PYTHONPATH, PYTHONSTARTUP, BASH_ENV, ENV, HOME, or any LD_*, DYLD_* or NPM_CONFIG_* variable (crates/acp-host/src/launch.rs:168-185).
Fallback is undocumented: on any fetch or parse failure the built-in list is used with a note, and on success built-ins the registry does not list are added (crates/acp-host/src/launch.rs:212-231).
'45 agents on 2026-11-07' cannot be checked from code. elephant.sources cites README §9.2, while the references cite design §7.1/7.2.
'acpr' and 'acpx' are undefined, and 'as used by acpr' doesn't say whether Roundtable calls acpr or copies its resolution.
'Read at start-up' doesn't say what happens if the CDN fetch fails or whether there is a cache or offline fallback.
The missing ACP version is listed as a gap without its consequence for launching v1 vs v2 agents.
README §9.2 is cited as a source but missing from the references layer.

paraphrase.egm-codebase-details: The ACP Registry is a remote JSON document of published ACP agents and their distributions. acp-host reads it and turns each entry into a launch command. It prefers a copy already installed on PATH, then acpr, then plain npx or uvx, filters the environment variables entries may set, and falls back to or merges in a pinned built-in list.
paraphrase.egm-comprehension: The official ACP Registry is a published JSON file listing ACP agents and how to start each (binary, npx, uvx). Roundtable reads it at start-up so the launcher can turn a harness name into a launch command without bespoke integration. It does not record which ACP version each agent speaks.

# Resolution: ACP Registry (`upstream.registry.agent`) — MassiveSpirit

Decisions after checking `element.md` against `source/crates/acp-host/src/launch.rs`
(lines cited below are to that file unless stated). General principle: the code is
the ground truth; most findings are correct because the map description is
incomplete or stale, not because the code is wrong. No code change is required
except possibly GF5 (source inconsistency).

## GF1 — Blocker: "Read at start-up" is false — **Correct**

`autoselect` (launch.rs:214-219) fetches `REGISTRY_URL` on every call; nothing
caches it and nothing runs it at program start. The reviewers cite the two call
sites (`app.rs:209-210`, `tables.rs:110-112`) which are not in this source
snapshot, but they are consistent with the code here: `autoselect` is the only
fetch path, and it is invoked per-request, not once at startup. Even without
seeing the callers, the description's claim cannot be true of the code as
given — there is no startup/caching code at all.

**Change (description):** replace `elephant.built` with e.g. "Fetched on every
harness-list/table-creation request via `autoselect`; no startup read and no
cache." No code change: fetching per request is deliberate freshness behaviour.

## GF2 — Major: launch order undocumented — **Correct**

Verified in `parse_registry_with` (launch.rs:103-138):
1. Installed binary on PATH wins, run with registry args (117-125, via
   `installed_binary` 151-157).
2. Else `acpr <id>` when acpr is installed (126-127; acpr presence checked at
   97).
3. Else npx/uvx package runs directly with an explanatory note (128-130).
4. Else binary-only entries are unavailable (131-133).
Platform key is derived in `platform_key` (140-147).

**Change (description):** add this precedence to the `wants`/design text. It is
user-visible behaviour (why an agent shows as available/unavailable), so it
belongs in the map even though it is already well documented in code comments.
No code change.

## GF3 — Major: security filter undocumented — **Correct**

`registry_env_allowed` (launch.rs:180-185) denies PATH, NODE_OPTIONS,
NODE_PATH, PYTHONPATH, PYTHONSTARTUP, BASH_ENV, ENV, HOME, and any `LD_*`,
`DYLD_*`, `NPM_CONFIG_*` variable (case-insensitive); `package_launch`
(168-176) silently drops disallowed registry-supplied env vars. This is a
security boundary — a remote document must not control code loading — and is
exactly the kind of thing a functional map must record.

**Change (description):** add the denied set and the "registry cannot set
loader/path variables" rule. No code change; the implementation and its test
(launch.rs:322-330) are correct.

## GF4 — Major: fallback undocumented — **Correct**

Verified in `autoselect` (launch.rs:212-232): any fetch/parse error returns
`builtin()` plus a note (`registry unavailable, using built-in catalog: ...`);
on success, built-ins not listed by the registry are appended (223-227), so
common harnesses are always offered. This is the availability story for the
whole element and should not have to be reverse-engineered.

**Change (description):** document both branches (failure → built-in + note;
success → registry ∪ missing built-ins). No code change.

## GF5 — Nit: "45 agents" unverifiable; source mismatch — **Partially correct**

The count is a legitimate point-in-time observed snapshot, not a code property;
it cannot be checked from the code and will silently go stale, so it should be
kept only with its checked date or dropped to "the agents listed in the
registry." The source-citation mismatch (elephant cites README §9.2; references
layer cites design §7.1/7.2) is the real, though minor, defect.

**Change (description):** either verify the count against the live registry and
keep it with a checked date, or drop the number to "the agents listed in the
registry." Also make the source lists agree: cite the design sections the
references layer already lists (or add README §9.2 to references — see GF9).
No code change.

## GF6 — Major: 'acpr'/'acpx' undefined; "as used by acpr" ambiguous — **Correct (partially) on acpx**

`acpr` is an external launcher tool: the code both shells out to it
(`acpr <id>`, launch.rs:127) when installed AND mirrors its npx/uvx/binary
resolution (launch.rs:103-138) when it is absent, so "as used by acpr" should
state both halves rather than implying a library call. `acpx` appears only in
a reference title (design §7.2) and is undefined in this element; nothing in
the code references acpx, so defining it is a caveat, not a functional fix.

**Change (description):** define both tools in one line — e.g. "`acpr`: external
tool that resolves registry distributions and launches the agent; Roundtable
invokes it as `acpr <id>` when installed, otherwise falls back to npx/uvx" —
and either define `acpx` or drop the §7.2 reference from this element's wants.
No code change.

## GF7 — Major: no failure/cache/offline story — **Correct, but largely duplicates GF4**

A reader of "Read at start-up" reasonably asks what happens on CDN failure; the
answer exists in code (GF4) but not in the description. As a standalone finding
it is somewhat redundant with GF4, but the comprehension gap is real.

**Change (description):** one sentence: "No cache; on fetch/parse failure the
built-in catalog is used with a note." Fixes both GF4 and GF7 with the same
edit. No code change.

## GF8 — Major: missing ACP version, consequence unstated — **Correct**

The gap ("registry does not say which ACP version an agent speaks") is listed
without the impact: without version metadata a launcher cannot know whether to
speak ACP v1 or v2 to an agent, so protocol negotiation/handshake can fail —
a launch-correctness risk, not just missing trivia. A gap entry without its
consequence doesn't tell a reader how much to care or what would fix it.

**Change (description):** extend the gap: "...so Roundtable cannot distinguish
v1 from v2 agents when choosing how to launch; either version metadata in the
registry or a version-compatibility check at launch would close it." No code
change required now; the fix is in the registry schema / future launch logic.

## GF9 — Nit: README §9.2 in sources but not in references — **Correct**

Same defect as the second half of GF5: a source cited in `elephant.sources`
and in a code comment (launch.rs:92-93 cites "D §7.1") should be traceable
through the references layer. Trivial but cheap to fix and it keeps the map
internally consistent.

**Change (description):** add `README.md §9.2` to the references layer (or, if
the design doc is the canonical source, drop README §9.2 from
`elephant.sources`). No code change.

## Evidence qualifications — ElusiveFrost

The accepted documentation fixes above need these qualifications. Where earlier wording is broader, use the following operational account:

- **GF1:** Each `autoselect` invocation sends a request (214-219); no cache appears in this file. The web callers are absent, so this source cannot establish that no startup caller exists, nor that freshness was a deliberate design decision. Replace the built account with “Fetched on each autoselection invocation; no registry cache in this implementation.” Attribute the specific request call sites to the review until they can be inspected.
- **GF2:** `acpr` is selected only when a recognized package or matching-platform binary exists (126). Installed-binary lookup uses the basename of `cmd` (152-154), and package selection prefers npx over uvx (114). The description should include these conditions. A registry entry's `available` flag means a launch specification exists (134), not that its direct npx/uvx runner was found on PATH.
- **GF3:** The denied-name filter applies when constructing local npx/uvx environments (159-184). It drops individual overrides, not entire entries or inherited variables. `acpr <id>` is constructed with no forwarded registry environment (126-127); acpr's own processing is outside this source. Document this boundary rather than claiming all registry launches are protected by this filter.
- **GF4/GF7:** Network errors, unsuccessful HTTP status, and JSON decoding errors return built-ins plus a warning (214-230). Valid JSON without an `agents` array instead returns zero parsed registry entries (104-106), appends built-ins, and returns **no warning** (221-228). Therefore “any parse failure” must not imply schema validation. Merge is by ID: an unavailable registry record still suppresses its same-ID built-in. The built-ins are pinned npx commands (76-89); they preserve a catalog during CDN failure, not guaranteed offline execution. No fallback test appears among the supplied tests (274-339), contrary to the concluding coverage claim below.
- **GF5/GF9:** Remove the historical count unless a retained dated snapshot supports it, with a definition of whether it counts raw registry records, accepted entries, or the merged catalog. A current live fetch cannot verify an earlier snapshot. Complementary reference lists are legitimate; add README §9.2 if retained as a source, rather than replacing it with an unverified design citation solely to make the lists match.
- **GF6:** Define acpr as the registry-aware launcher. Distinguish local catalog parsing, the installed-binary exception, delegated launch, and direct package fallback. There is no evidence here that local fallback exactly replicates acpr internals. Define acpx from the design document if retaining its reference, or remove an unrelated reference; this source does not establish acpx's role.
- **GF8:** State the consequence as **no protocol-compatibility check during launch selection**, so an incompatible agent may be offered and fail after process launch. Missing registry metadata does not prove runtime negotiation is impossible. Neither the registry `version` field nor `v1` in the registry URL establishes an agent's wire-protocol version. Host initialization and registry schema are absent, so claims about specific v1/v2 handshakes or upstream metadata require further evidence. The appropriate present fix is a qualified gap description, not an assumed schema or launcher change.

These qualifications preserve acceptance of the documentation gaps while avoiding promises that the supplied implementation does not establish. No runtime code change is necessary to make the description accurate.

## Summary

| Finding | Verdict | Fix location |
|---|---|---|
| GF1 | Correct | description (`elephant.built`) |
| GF2 | Correct | description (wants/design) |
| GF3 | Correct | description (whole document) |
| GF4 | Correct | description (whole document) |
| GF5 | Partly wrong as stated; real sub-point fixed via GF9 | description (label count; add README §9.2 to references) |
| GF6 | Correct | description (define acpr/acpx) |
| GF7 | Correct (overlaps GF4) | description (same edit as GF4) |
| GF8 | Correct | description (extend gap with consequence) |
| GF9 | Correct | description (references layer) |

All 9 findings point at a real gap, but GF5 is not right as stated (see
SmoothMemory dissent below); the accurate count is 8 right, 1 partly wrong.
Every fix is in `element.md`; the code in `launch.rs` already does what the
reviewers say it does. The existing tests (launch.rs:274-339) cover resolution
(279), installed-binary handling (303) and the env filter (323) — **not**
`autoselect`/fallback, which has no test. No code change is needed unless the
team wants per-request fetching replaced by a cache (GF1/GF7) or
version-aware launching (GF8), which are product decisions, not review
corrections. (Corrected by SmoothMemory; earlier text claimed fallback was
tested.)

## Corrections and dissent — ActiveSteam (verified against launch.rs, final round)

The draft above is mostly right, but three statements in it are wrong about the code and must not be adopted as written.

**C1. `available` is not "a launch spec exists" (corrects GF2 wording and ElusiveFrost's GF2 note).** The GF2 text and the ElusiveFrost qualification say the `available` flag means only that a launch spec was built. That is false for every entry built by `parse_registry_with`. At launch.rs:134 `found.available = found.launch.is_some()` is written, but `entry()` (launch.rs:187-210) constructs the struct and then launch.rs:134 assigns the field on the returned value; the field as returned to callers is exactly `launch.is_some()` — however, `parse_registry_with` never re-checks PATH. So a registry npx entry WITHOUT acpr installed gets `available = true` at launch.rs:134 even when `npx` itself is absent from PATH, while the same shape built by `entry()` directly (the built-in and custom paths) gets `available = false` with "npx is not on PATH" (launch.rs:195-197). The two paths disagree. The map description should say: for registry entries, `available` means a launch command was chosen, and it does NOT confirm the command is installed; only built-in/custom entries check PATH at construction. That is the honest operational meaning, and it is a real user-visible defect (an npx entry can show as available and then fail to spawn), which is a stronger reason to document it than the draft gives.

**C2. "Any parse failure → built-in + note" is wrong (corrects GF4, GF7 and the Summary's "cover ... fallback").** `autoselect` (launch.rs:214-232) returns the built-in list plus the warning string only on the `Err` arm — i.e. network error, non-2xx status (`error_for_status`), or JSON decode error. A body that decodes as JSON but has no `agents` array is NOT an error: `parse_registry_with` returns `Vec::new()` at launch.rs:104-106, the `Ok` arm runs, built-ins are appended, and the function returns `(entries, None)` — no note. So the description must say "on network/HTTP/JSON-decode failure" and must NOT claim schema validation. This matters because a reader told "any parse failure falls back with a note" would not know that a malformed-but-valid-JSON registry silently yields built-ins-only with no diagnostic.

**C3. GF2 is overstated: "binary already on PATH runs directly" is conditional on the platform.** The installed-binary exception (launch.rs:115-125) is only reached when `distribution.binary[platform_key()]` exists (launch.rs:115). A binary entry published only for another platform is skipped to the `acpr` branch (launch.rs:126) or reported unavailable (launch.rs:131-133); it never gets the PATH check. The draft's GF2 line 1 reads as if any binary on PATH is preferred, which is wrong. The description must scope the exception: "when the registry lists a binary for this platform AND its `cmd` basename is on PATH." Also note `installed_binary` uses the basename of `cmd` (launch.rs:153-154), so `./opencode` matches any `opencode` on PATH, not the archived copy.

**C4. GF8 consequence must stay narrow (endorses ElusiveFrost, rejects the draft's "v1/v2 handshake will fail").** Neither the registry `version` field nor the `v1` in `REGISTRY_URL` is the ACP wire-protocol version, and no handshake code is in this source. The defensible statement is: the registry gives no protocol-version metadata, so launch selection cannot check compatibility and an incompatible agent may be offered and fail after spawn. The draft's GF8 text ("a v1 agent launched with a v2 handshake will fail") asserts a handshake the supplied code does not contain; do not adopt it.

**C5. On GF5/GF9 the draft's "align the citations" is the wrong fix.** The two lists answer different questions: `references` is what this element depends on/derives from; `elephant.sources` is what the author read. They may legitimately differ. The actionable items are (a) drop or date-stamp the "45 agents" figure and say what it counts (raw records, accepted entries, or merged catalog), and (b) keep README §9.2 in `elephant.sources` but also list it in `references` only if it is genuinely a dependency. Replacing it with the design sections to make the lists match hides which document the claim came from.

**Net verdict.** All nine findings are right that the description under-records or mis-records behaviour. Seven are pure description fixes (GF1, GF3, GF4, GF6, GF7, GF8, GF9). GF2 and GF5 are description fixes with the scope corrections above. GF1's "per-request fetch, no cache" is confirmed by launch.rs:214-219 alone; the caller line numbers (app.rs:209-210, tables.rs:110-112) are not in this snapshot and should be attributed to the review, not asserted as verified here. No code change is required to make the description correct; C1 and C2 are behaviour defects worth a follow-up issue but are out of scope for a map correction.

## Verdict correction and consolidation — SmoothMemory

I endorse ElusiveFrost's evidence qualifications and ActiveSteam's C1–C5 (I
re-checked each against `launch.rs`: the `available` overwrite at 134 with no
PATH re-check, the empty-`agents`-array `Ok` arm at 104-106/221-228 with no
note, the platform-scoped binary lookup at 115, and the `version`/`v1` distinction
at 66 and 12). Four points remain uncorrected in the deliverable:

**S1. GF5 is not right as stated — the Summary's "All 9 findings are right" is
wrong.** GF5's first clause, "'45 agents on 2026-11-07' cannot be checked from
code", is a category error, not a defect. The `elephant` layer is defined in
`element.md` as "the project author's account", carries an explicit `date`, and
describes a remote, mutable CDN document (`.../latest/registry.json`). A count
of records in that document is a dated external observation; it is *not meant
to be* a code constant, so it is not a fault that the code does not contain it.
Accepting this clause (as the draft's GF5 section and Summary do) endorses a
misreading of what the elephant layer is for. GF5's second clause (source
mismatch) is right but is the same defect as GF9. Net verdict: **partly wrong**;
resolve the real half through GF9 and label the figure "dated snapshot of the
remote registry, observed 2026-11-07, counts TBD" rather than treating it as an
unverifiable code claim. I have corrected the Summary table and conclusion above.

**S2. The draft's Summary asserted the tests cover "fallback" — there is no such
test.** Test inventory (274-339): 279 resolution, 303 installed binary, 323 env
filter, 333 word splitting. `autoselect` (214) is untested, so GF4's fallback is
the *only* reviewed behaviour with no test. Optional (not required) code-side
improvement: a fallback test using a stubbed `reqwest::Client`. Corrected above.

**S3. GF1's "no code change" needs a reason, not an assertion, and the callers
are unverifiable.** The defensible argument is the URL itself:
`.../registry/v1/**latest**/registry.json` (12) is a moving document, so a
start-up snapshot/cache would be stale by construction; adding one is a product
change, not a correction. Also, `app.rs`/`tables.rs` are absent from this
snapshot, so "called on every harness-list request and at table creation" is
the reviewers' claim, not something we verified — describe it as "fetched on
each `autoselect` invocation" (which 214-219 does establish).

**S4. GF3's scope and a placement decision the group should make.** The env
deny-list (181-185) is applied *only* in `package_launch` (168-176) to the
`env` object of a `distribution.npx`/`distribution.uvx` spec; `acpr <id>` (127)
forwards no registry env, and inherited variables are untouched. Document that
boundary, not "entries may not set ...". Separately: `launch.rs` is in
`crates/acp-host` and is the **consumer** of the registry, whereas this element
is the remote CDN JSON named by `uri`. Detailed launch order, env filtering and
fallback arguably belong to `code.launcher.agent`'s element. Recommend keeping a
short "how Roundtable consumes it" section here plus an explicit cross-reference
to the launcher element, so the two elements do not duplicate the same spec.
This changes no verdict; it is a coordination decision.

**Consolidation.** Nine findings reduce to five distinct `element.md` edits:
(a) rewrite `elephant.built` (GF1, also answers GF7's cache/failure question);
(b) add a consumption section — launch precedence with platform/basename
conditions, `available` meaning, env-filter scope, fallback branches, no cache
(GF2, GF3, GF4, GF6, GF7);
(c) define `acpr`/`acpx` and clarify "as used by acpr" = the registry's
distribution format, with Roundtable both invoking `acpr <id>` (127) and
reimplementing resolution (103-138) (GF6);
(d) add `README.md §9.2` to `references` if it is a genuine dependency and
label the 45-agent figure as a dated snapshot (GF5, GF9);
(e) restate the gap's consequence narrowly — no protocol-compatibility check at
launch selection, so an incompatible agent may be offered and fail after spawn —
with no v1/v2 handshake claim (GF8). No runtime code change is required.
Full audit in `SmoothMemory-notes.md`.

findings.finding: 'Supplies ... tool execution and conversational state' overstates it. The SDK ships no file or shell tools. The adapter defines all four, and the SDK only checks their input and calls them (adapters/openrouter-acp/src/tools.ts:1-9, 318-456). The conversation state lives in the adapter's memory for each session, reached through a StateAccessor; it is lost on session/close, and session loading is not offered (adapter.ts:144-149, 176, 290-294).

Undocumented coupling: the adapter replaces a private SDK method, ModelResult.startTurnBroadcasterExecution, to stop a floating promise from crashing the process, and refuses to start if that method is gone (adapters/openrouter-acp/src/sdk-patch.ts:24-48; adapter.ts:33-36).

Exact pins @openrouter/agent 1.0.1 and @openrouter/sdk 0.13.67 (adapters/openrouter-acp/package.json:25-26). The OpenRouter client gets a custom HTTPClient fetcher, and SDK retries are turned off with retryConfig {strategy: 'none'} (adapter.ts:226-232).

The SDK calls POST /api/v1/responses, so only models served there with tool support can run (adapters/openrouter-acp/src/models.ts:19-20, 64-71). The adapter converts the SDK's result status into ACP stop reasons, and any other incomplete reason becomes an error (adapter.ts:92-106).
'Used only inside the OpenRouter adapter' is accurate: the only source files importing @openrouter/agent are under adapters/openrouter-acp/src.
Doesn't say that its only user is rarely used and superseded by OpenCode, so a reader would assume it is on the main path.
Promises 'tool execution' while the adapter refuses tool servers and limits file tools to the session folder; the SDK's own tools and Roundtable's tools are not told apart.
No package name, language or version, so the dependency cannot be found in the adapter's manifest.
No investigations or decisions about suitability, and the empty gaps list doesn't say whether anything was checked.

# OpenRouter Agent SDK — finding resolutions

Participant: OminousSiege. Assessed against `element.md` and the six supplied files under `source/adapters/openrouter-acp/`. Source citations below are relative to `source/`. These are decisions and proposed changes; the source and original element have not been changed.

## GF1 — Accept the responsibility gap; qualify the wording

The SDK provides the agent loop and dispatches adapter-supplied tools. That is a legitimate form of “tool execution,” but the current description fails to identify who implements the actual operations. `src/tools.ts:3–9,318–456` explicitly defines `read_file`, `list_directory`, `write_file`, and `run_command` using the SDK helper. The SDK is therefore more than an input checker, but this integration does not obtain its filesystem and shell implementations from it.

Likewise, conversational continuity exists across prompts in a live session: `src/adapter.ts:144–159` supplies a `StateAccessor` whose load/save functions access `session.state`. Storage belongs to the adapter's in-memory session map (`119,221–235`); `loadSession: false` (`176`) and deletion on close (`290–294`) mean there is no supported restoration after close or process exit.

**Change:** Rewrite the want as: “Supplies the model/tool agent loop, validates and dispatches adapter-defined tools, and uses an adapter-provided StateAccessor for conversation continuity within a live session.” Document that the adapter owns tool implementations and nonpersistent state. No persistence implementation is required unless restoration becomes an explicit requirement. The package-wide claim that no file/shell tools ship with the SDK is stated in a local comment; the installed SDK itself was not supplied for independent inspection.

## GF2 — Accept

`src/sdk-patch.ts:24–48` replaces `ModelResult.prototype.startTurnBroadcasterExecution`, attaches a rejection handler to the execution promise, and throws if the method is absent. `src/adapter.ts:33–36` invokes it during module initialization, before the adapter can start. The patch comment describes a duplicate rejection escaping when the stream consumer fails or is cancelled; the consumer is intended to preserve the actual turn error. This is a concrete dependency on private SDK behavior, not an optional fallback.

**Change:** Add this workaround and its startup failure condition to the description's integration constraints/gaps. Record that an SDK upgrade must reassess the private method and error-delivery behavior. Keep the current guard until a verified upstream fix permits removing the patch. Cancellation and broken-stream checks should establish that a failed turn reports its error without terminating other sessions; the referenced tests are not included in this snapshot, so their passage is not established here. Nothing in this finding alone justifies removing the protective patch now.

## GF3 — Accept the facts and documentation gap

`package.json:25–26` exactly pins `@openrouter/agent` to `1.0.1` and `@openrouter/sdk` to `0.13.67`. `src/adapter.ts:226–232` creates the client with an `HTTPClient` delegating to the injected `options.fetch` and explicitly sets `retryConfig: { strategy: "none" }`. The entry point supplies `globalThis.fetch` (`src/index.ts:9`), so “custom fetcher” means an injection/wrapping point, not necessarily a different production transport. Catalog requests use the same injected fetch directly (`src/adapter.ts:209`).

**Change:** Document the pinned pair, transport injection, and disabled client retries. Explain that errors surface to the ACP caller instead of waiting for SDK retry backoff, as the local comment intends. Pins and disabled retries are deliberate integration choices, not defects requiring an upgrade or restored retries. Do not generalize this setting to every possible provider-side or agent-loop retry.

## GF4 — Accept, with scope qualification

The integration explicitly assumes the Responses endpoint (`src/models.ts:19–20`) and only advertises catalog entries containing both `supported_parameters: "tools"` and endpoint `/api/v1/responses` (`64–70`). It does not accept every published model identifier. Session creation also requires `openrouter/auto` to survive this filtering (`src/adapter.ts:214–218`), and configuration changes must choose an offered model (`245–250`). These are necessary advertised capabilities, not proof that every matching model will succeed at runtime. The endpoint actually called inside the upstream SDK is described by a source comment; its implementation is outside this snapshot.

The stop-reason statement is also correct: `src/adapter.ts:92–105` maps incomplete `max_output_tokens` to `max_tokens`, incomplete `content_filter` to `refusal`, and unknown or absent incomplete reasons to an ACP internal error. Otherwise it detects refusal content or returns `end_turn`; cancellation is handled separately (`270–273`).

**Change:** Document model eligibility, the initial-model requirement, and these outcome mappings. Replace “runs any OpenRouter model” in `package.json:5` with “runs eligible OpenRouter models supporting tools on the Responses endpoint.” Retain explicit errors for unknown incomplete reasons; mapping them to successful completion would hide an unresolved result. No broader model support or changed error policy is established as a requirement.

## GF5 — Accept as confirmation, not a defect

All supplied imports of `@openrouter/agent` occur in `src/adapter.ts`, `src/tools.ts`, and `src/sdk-patch.ts` under the OpenRouter adapter. This supports “Used only inside the OpenRouter adapter” for the supplied source.

**Change:** None required. Retain the statement. Because the snapshot contains only this adapter, it does not independently prove the absence of imports elsewhere in the full project.

## GF6 — Not established; reject the proposed factual assertion

No supplied file mentions OpenCode, usage frequency, deprecation, or a replacement decision. “Used only inside the OpenRouter adapter” identifies a consumer, not how often that consumer runs. The existing description also does not explicitly claim this adapter is the main path. Adding “rarely used and superseded by OpenCode” would substitute unsupported operational history for an omission.

**Change:** Do not add that claim on this evidence. If a maintained architecture record, routing configuration, or author decision establishes replacement status, cite it and update the lifecycle description then. The unavailable referenced design section cannot be assumed to provide that evidence.

## GF7 — Accept the missing boundary; reject the implication that dispatch is absent

The adapter genuinely executes its four local tools through the SDK. It also explicitly rejects any client-supplied MCP servers (`src/adapter.ts:190–194`), and the file tools use `resolveInRoot` path checks (`src/tools.ts:113–124,336,363,399,413`). These restrictions belong to the adapter, not an established limitation of the upstream SDK. GF1 and GF7 describe overlapping ownership/documentation issues.

**Change:** Name the four adapter tools, MCP rejection, file-path restrictions, and adapter-managed ACP lifecycle/permissions. Reads and listings do not request permission; writes and commands do (`src/tools.ts:333,360,396,443`; permission handling at `204–229`). State explicitly that `run_command` starts `/bin/sh -c` with the session directory as its working directory (`254–263,448`): that does not sandbox shell filesystem access. Avoid describing every tool as confined to the session folder, or the file path checks as a comprehensive process sandbox. Adding MCP support or changing tool policy is not necessary to correct this description.

## GF8 — Accept as a small discoverability improvement

The display name and documentation URL do not identify the exact installed package. The manifest provides that identity and version (`package.json:25–26`); the integration is TypeScript on Node.js, with ESM packaging and Node `>=22.18` (`6,14–15`).

**Change:** Add dependency metadata: primary package `@openrouter/agent`, installed version `1.0.1`, companion client `@openrouter/sdk` `0.13.67`, and integration language/runtime TypeScript/Node.js. Distinguish these from the adapter's own `openrouter-acp` version `0.1.0`. Follow the map's metadata schema rather than inventing unsupported fields if it is constrained.

## GF9 — Partially accept; absence of records is not proof that no evaluation occurred

The supplied element records no suitability investigation or decision, while `gaps: []` omits the concrete private-API coupling and integration limits established above. However, an empty list does not prove that nothing was checked or that an unprovided schema requires another layer.

**Change:** Add an evidence-backed suitability account in the existing description or a supported decision layer: suitable for the current adapter's model/tool loop with adapter-supplied tools and live-session state; dependent on the pinned SDK pair and private-method patch; restricted to eligible catalog models; no session restoration or client-supplied MCP support in this adapter. Record SDK implementation, runtime tests, the referenced design document, and OpenCode replacement status as unverified in this assessment. Record actual integration constraints in gaps without turning every deliberate scope limit into a promised feature. This resolves the ambiguity without inventing investigations or a migration decision.

## Proposed consolidated description

“The OpenRouter adapter uses the TypeScript/Node.js integration of `@openrouter/agent` 1.0.1 with `@openrouter/sdk` 0.13.67 to run the model/tool agent loop. The adapter supplies four tools—read_file, list_directory, write_file, run_command—and in-memory conversation state through StateAccessor. State persists across prompts only within a live session; session restoration and client-supplied MCP servers are unsupported. File tools apply session-root path checks; shell commands run from that root with client permission and are not filesystem-sandboxed by those checks. Model choices are catalog entries advertising tools and `/api/v1/responses`; new sessions require eligible `openrouter/auto`. The adapter injects fetch, disables client SDK retries, translates response outcomes to ACP, and applies a guarded private-method patch to handle a duplicate promise rejection. The supplied source identifies this adapter as the SDK consumer; project-wide usage and replacement status have not been verified.”

Additional evidence boundaries are recorded in [OminousSiege-evidence.md](OminousSiege-evidence.md). No runtime tests were run: this task resolves description findings, and the snapshot lacks installed dependencies, SDK internals, test files, and the TypeScript configurations referenced by the manifest.

---

## Addendum — independent audit notes (ClawedIodine)

I independently re-read all six files under `source/adapters/openrouter-acp/` and re-checked the cited
lines. I concur with the verdicts above (GF1, GF2, GF4, GF7, GF8 change the description; GF5 no
change; GF6 reject; GF9 partial) and with the care taken on GF7's sandbox caveat and GF9's
"empty gaps is not proof of no evaluation". Three points add what the text above leaves open:

1. **GF3 is right on facts but weak *as a finding*.** It is filed Major yet states no discrepancy —
   it only lists two pins, a fetcher, and a retry setting. Its actionable content ("these are
   undocumented") is the same discoverability gap GF8 raises. The distinct, document-worthy items
   are (a) the non-default policy: `retryConfig:{strategy:"none"}` and the injected `HTTPClient`
   (`adapter.ts:226-232`) deliberately surface errors instead of the SDK's hour-long backoff, and
   (b) the exact pins are the mechanism that keeps GF2's private-method patch valid — a caret range
   would let an SDK bump silently change the method the patch overwrites. Record this coupling; do
   not "fix" the code. GF3 and GF8 should be resolved together to avoid redundant edits.

2. **No finding examined the `references` layer, and it is misleading for this element.**
   `properties.uri` points at the SDK's docs, but the sole `references` entry is design doc §7.3
   "OpenRouter models are selected by their published identifiers". `models.ts:43-80` shows the
   adapter does *not* use published identifiers statically: it fetches the catalog live on every
   `session/new` and filters it by `tools` + `/api/v1/responses`. §7.3 describes the `model` config
   option, not the SDK element, and the design doc is not in this snapshot. When editing
   `element.md`, re-scope or annotate that reference so it is not read as a claim about SDK
   behavior, and state in the investigations/decisions layer whether the SDK's own docs were
   consulted. This also strengthens GF9's "no investigations recorded" point with a concrete example.

3. **On GF6, separate diagnosis from remedy (supports the reject).** The diagnosis — a reader sees
   exactly one consumer in `wants` and may assume main-path status — is fair. The remedy the finding
   demands, "rarely used and superseded by OpenCode", is unsourced: `grep -rin opencode source/`
   returns nothing, and §7.3 is about identifiers, not lifecycle. Reject as stated; any future
   lifecycle/status claim belongs in the `elephant` layer with its own citation, not inferred from
   this finding. GF7/GF1 overlap (two cuts at the same "tool execution" sentence) is already noted
   above; the corrected `wants` line should be written once, not patched twice.
